comment_en: Your center of gravity is too high, and the wrist and upper arm direct too much force upward. Stabilize the connection between your wrist and forearm, then direct the upper arm, forearm, and wrist forward rather than upward. Keep the wrist firm when applying force instead of letting it become too loose.

You lean backward after hitting; instead, keep your weight pressing forward. Relax the shoulder and forearm, and let the shoulder settle rather than lifting it. Bring the forearm back toward the nose or eye level instead of above the head. Keep this a controlled recovery movement and reduce the excessive movement of your trunk.

Your center of gravity is too far back. Lean your torso forward slightly and bend your knees more. Wrist stability has improved, but when applying force, you still tend to direct it upward; control your wrist and direct the force forward. Your upper arm moves too much and needs better control during the forward movement. Waist rotation is insufficient, and you rely too heavily on your shoulder to execute the stroke.

Your upper arm remains somewhat stiff, and your body tilts upward after hitting. Draw the forearm backward and rotate your waist to the right. Keep your weight controlled and forward, avoiding an upward tilt after the stroke. Stabilize the wrist while using its strength to turn upward.
Your wrist tilts too far to the left; direct its force forward and keep the racket head down. Bend your right knee more. Hip rotation has improved.

Relax and lower your shoulder. Rotate your waist farther to the right while drawing the racket backward. Finish consistently in front of your nose instead of bringing the hand toward the shoulder or above the head. Remove unnecessary movements and recover along a shorter path rather than making circles. Reduce the excessive wrist movement and keep the action more compact.
You use too much upper-arm force after contact, causing the elbow to straighten. Lean your upper body forward over the table when striking.

Your forearm and wrist are too tense, and wrist movement is insufficient. Relax them, draw the forearm and racket farther backward, and use more wrist action. Keep the racket face flatter, brush the lower part of the ball, and apply forward force. Step in earlier and establish firm footing before applying force. Bring your shoulders, neck, and head forward with your weight instead of leaving them behind.
Your upper-body posture is too high, and your waist is too upright.

Your contact point is too far back; meet the ball farther forward. Step in earlier, settle downward, and relax your forearm. Avoid straightening and tensing your whole body after contact; keep the shoulders relaxed as well. Moving your body half a step forward would help establish the intended contact position.

Your center of gravity is too high, so bend your knees more. The forearm drops too low during the backswing, restricting backward waist rotation. Raise the forearm and use your waist and hips to carry the arm backward. Direct the force forward through contact rather than upward.

Your topspin stroke is generally good, but the neck and head remain stiff; relax them. Rotate your waist farther to the right during the backswing to support a freer application of force. Recover downward immediately after hitting rather than pausing to watch the ball.

Bend your knees more and lean your upper body farther forward. Raise the wrist before contact and use your waist and hips to turn backward rather than simply dropping the arm downward. Then rotate from back to front and direct the force forward. The current overall movement is too upward.

You rely too much on arm strength. Rotate your waist to the right and transfer that rotational force into the arm. Replace the circular arm path with a direct diagonal movement out and back; the circular action slows recovery. Make the stroke cleaner and more compact, and move the contact point farther forward.

Use your upper body to press over the ball during contact rather than making a downward smashing action. Raise the forearm during the backswing and move from back to front instead of drawing it downward. The notes also say that the hand does not tilt back enough and does not tilt forward enough, without distinguishing the intended phases.
review_notes: The hand-tilt instructions conflict or lack phase context; retain for review rather than resolve by guessing.

comment_en: You are transferring waist rotation into the arm more effectively, and the stroke has a better sense of tightening through contact. However, the movement still follows a circular path. Relax and use a cleaner diagonal path upward and back downward with waist rotation. Relax your shoulders, neck, and head, and let them follow the ball. Keep your weight forward after hitting instead of straightening and tensing the body or leaving the neck tilted backward.
Your application of force and the timing of brushing contact have improved. However, your upper body remains too high, and the right knee does not bend enough.

The stroke still looks like a push rather than a sharp downward brushing action driven by the wrist. Strengthen the brief wrist action from the backswing into the downward cut, contacting the lower side of the ball. Bring your weight farther forward and lower your posture more.

The overall action has improved, but your center of gravity remains too high; bend your knees more. The arm now travels farther backward, yet hip rotation is still limited. During the backswing, let the waist lead the shoulders instead of using the arm to pull the waist around.

You brush too strongly upward, causing the ball to travel long. Press the forearm action and your weight farther forward. Allow more time for the backswing and waist rotation so that the ball rises higher before contact; you currently strike too early. Forearm closing is good, but waist rotation is not yet contributing fully to the stroke.

Your center of gravity is too high. Bend your knees and lean forward at the waist. Increase backward waist rotation during the backswing, feeling the right knee turn to the right. Let the lower body lead the hips and waist into the backswing, maintaining a connected movement from ankle to shoulder.
You use the shoulders too much. Relax them and avoid excessive lifting. Let the shoulder connect the waist and arm without pressing it downward excessively.

Your balance is unstable, as though you are standing on one leg during contact. Adjust both feet to find the ball instead of remaining fixed. Reduce excessive wrist movement, stabilize the forearm, and use a brief burst of wrist force to brush the bottom of the ball. Your contact timing is good.

Your stance is too square; place the right foot forward. Stabilize the wrist-to-forearm angle during contact. The middle, ring, and little fingers are too loose, so grip the racket more firmly. Contact the ball on the upper-right area of the racket rather than the lower-left area.

Your body still sways during contact; establish firmer footing. Reduce wrist wobble and use a smaller, more explosive wrist action. The wrist is held too close to the body in a cramped position, making the movement awkward.

Your grip is incorrect: the fingers and palm do not hold the racket firmly during force application, while the forearm contributes too much. Your waist is too upright; lean your weight forward and slightly to the right. Feel the toes of the right foot gripping the ground.

Your rhythm is good, and your foot positioning has improved. However, keep adjusting both feet rather than remaining in one place. Reduce excessive body sway and use footwork to bring your body forward to the contact point. Reduce the wrist's movement range and produce a firm burst of force with a smaller action.

Direct your weight forward and to the right instead of leaning left after contact. Wrap all fingers firmly around the handle, especially the middle, ring, and little fingers, which currently only rest against its side. Reduce excessive forearm force and maintain a straight, approximately 180-degree alignment between the wrist and forearm while gripping the racket firmly.

Your wrist, forearm, and shoulder are stiff and tend to lift upward. Maintain a stable shoulder and upper-arm position with only enough tension to support it. Make the forearm-closing action more pronounced, rotate your waist to the right without lifting the shoulder, and wait slightly longer before contacting the ball.

Weight transfer is insufficient. The coach asks you to establish weight over the left knee before moving it toward the right knee, rather than moving directly from the middle to the left. Your wrist is also raised too high; keep it aligned with the forearm at approximately 180 degrees during contact.

You do not hold the racket firmly enough, leaving a gap between the handle and the web of the hand. The wrist is stiff. Relax the forearm, bring your shoulder and weight forward, and contact the ball slightly later.

Your weight transfer has improved. The wrist still moves slightly during contact; lower it a little and feel the index finger supporting the racket face. Relax the left hand and hold it beside your body rather than pressed against the front of your torso.
Let the wrist relax before tightening it to apply force, rather than keeping it tense throughout the movement.

Your center of gravity is too high, causing an excessively high forearm backswing. Bend your knees more to establish a better contact position, and lower the wrist slightly during contact. Both wrist control and weight transfer have improved compared with the previous video.

Your whole body is too tense, and you lean forward too rigidly. Relax and use more of the wrist's brief explosive force at contact. Footwork is insufficient: step the right foot forward and then recover.
review_notes: A fragment about backswing distance is unclear and was omitted.

comment_en: Your center of gravity is too high; lean forward at the waist. Step the right foot into the table and keep your weight over the right forefoot during contact. The backswing is too large, so make the action more compact and emphasize the forward movement rather than excessive backward preparation.

You are not stepping forward to transfer your weight. The forearm backswing is too large, moving the contact point progressively backward. Meet the ball farther forward, shorten the forearm action, use more wrist force, and lean your body slightly forward.
Move the whole action forward. Your center of gravity is too high, particularly through the waist.

Your backswing reaches too far toward the shoulder. Shorten it and use the wrist's brief explosive action to cut forward, with less forearm involvement. Improve footwork and lean forward to find the contact point with your body rather than reaching for the ball with the arm alone.

The backswing is too large, and the wrist swings excessively. Shift your weight slightly forward and right, bringing your body toward the table. The coach emphasizes using the upper-right contact area instead of the left or lower-left area of the racket.
review_notes: The contact-area wording switches between ball and racket; its exact referent needs checking.

comment_en: Your left hand is too stiff; let it rest beside your body. The waist is also rigid and contributes little force. Bring both the forearm and waist into the stroke.

Your center of gravity is too high and too far toward your heels. Bend your knees, lean forward at the waist, and feel your toes gripping the ground. The transfer movement is reasonably good, but complete the forearm follow-through toward eyebrow level.
review_notes: The transcription of the exact eyebrow-side target is unclear.

comment_en: You stand too upright and stiffly. Bring both shoulders and your weight forward, and rotate the right side of your waist farther to the right. Keep the hand stable, draw the racket farther back, and relax and open the elbow before closing the forearm with waist rotation. Complete the follow-through while maintaining a forward lean.
review_notes: The specified follow-through endpoint is unintelligible in the source and was not reconstructed.

comment_en: Your body is stiff during contact, with insufficient knee bend and forward lean. However, your contact point is well controlled. Complete the forearm movement more fully, finishing near the left eyebrow.

After hitting, face the table and maintain a controlled forward lean instead of standing upright or rotating too far left. Increase the backward preparation of the racket so that you can produce a stronger burst of force at contact.

The first two strokes are incomplete, but wrist and forearm movement improve later in the round. Your center of gravity remains too high, especially in the lower body, and too far toward the heels. Lean your body farther forward and feel the forefeet gripping the ground.
Your body becomes increasingly stiff. Use a brief burst of wrist force to cut downward rather than lifting forward; this should improve the quality of the push.
Keep the racket face flatter rather than too upright. Wrap the fingers more fully around the racket during brushing contact instead of relying only on the thumb and index finger.

Move the hand forward, keep the racket face flatter, and brush the lower part of the ball. Avoid rushing and relax the stiff shoulder. Your contact point is moving too far backward; bring it forward again.

Your forearm force application has improved, but finger use remains a problem. Grip the racket handle firmly with the whole hand, wrapping the supporting fingers around it rather than relying on a partial grip. Better finger control should improve the force delivered to the ball.

Your shoulders move too much. Relax them and let them follow your body. Open the elbow and use the forearm to brush the ball. During the backswing, lower the hand beside the right thigh, then strike and brush upward from below. Keep your body pressing forward after contact.

Wrap the supporting fingers around the handle instead of relying only on the thumb and index finger. Shift your weight left and rotate the waist backward. The backswing angle between the forearm and upper arm is insufficient.

Your contact timing is good, and waist rotation is present, but it remains too limited to contribute enough force. Reduce excessive shoulder movement and the oversized arm swing; do not swing the hand behind your hips. Relax, finish in front of your nose rather than beside the left ear, and tilt the racket to brush the ball more. Correct the grip: the index finger extends too high, and the wrist wobbles on every stroke.

Let your waist lead the shoulder into the backswing and through contact, rather than using the shoulder to pull the waist around. Rightward waist rotation is too small while the racket backswing is too large. This disconnects shoulder and waist force and prevents it from concentrating on the ball.

Your upper arm and the joints from shoulder to elbow are too stiff. Begin the serve relaxed and tighten only when applying force. Wrist action improves later in the round, helping you brush the bottom of the ball. Serve one ball at a time instead of rushing. Place the ball in the center of the left palm, not near the finger bases. Coordinate waist rotation and forearm action rather than relying entirely on the arm.

Your center of gravity is too high, and your body turns only after the racket contacts the ball. Let the body lead the arm. If you intend to serve sidespin-topspin, use a more upright racket face; the current flatter angle produces sidespin-backspin. Turn the body more fully toward the front, including the finishing foot action. The toss is low and affects contact; toss slightly higher when attempting a long serve.
Your serve timing is incorrect because you rush into contact. The action lacks a relaxed-to-firm transition, limiting explosive force. Coordinate the waist and arm more effectively.

The serve is generally acceptable, but turn the right shoulder farther toward the front. The racket face is too flat; make it more upright, approximately 45 degrees, at contact. Hold the ball in the palm with the tossing fingers together and flat. Contact is sometimes too late, preventing waist force from aligning with the strike and making it difficult to serve long.

Your elbow and wrist are somewhat stiff, although the burst of wrist force is generally good. Contact occurs too late, when the ball has risen too high to control downward effectively. You push forward rather than cut downward. Keep the racket face flatter and use a brief wrist action to brush the lower part of the ball downward and create backspin instead of sending a relatively unspun ball forward.

The overall action is sound, but the wrist is raised too high, causing contact on the lower part of the racket. Use the upper-right area of the racket for better brushing contact. Your center of gravity is also too high and your waist too upright; lean your upper body forward.

Your wrist action is good, and the contact point has moved forward. However, the shoulder and forearm remain too stiff to produce sufficient instantaneous force. You still push from back to front rather than cutting downward. Brush the lower part of the ball with a brief downward action to produce backspin instead of a relatively unspun return.
Your center of gravity is too high. Let the forearm lead the whole hand through contact rather than applying force with the wrist alone. The racket face is too upright; keep it flatter.

Your step-in and recovery footwork have improved considerably, with better forward and backward weight movement. The contact point has also improved, and the ball trajectory is lower than before. Continue to brush the lower part of the ball with a downward cutting action rather than pushing it forward.

You contact the ball too far beyond its highest point, missing the best brushing timing. The racket face is too upright; flatten it slightly. Your waist is too straight, so keep your weight farther forward over the forefeet.

Your right shoulder is stiff and supplies too much of the force. Reduce shoulder effort and use more waist and abdominal rotation. The tightening action through contact is good, but stay relaxed during the backswing, then briefly tighten and grip the racket at contact before relaxing again.
The topspin action has no major problem, but your weight is too high and too far back over the heels. Bring it forward over the forefeet, soften the chest, and draw in the abdomen during the stroke.

You show a relaxed-to-firm transition and a clear concentration of force at contact, and the shoulder is less stiff than before. However, your weight rises too sharply from low to high, and the movements have become oversized, with more errors. When the waist rotates sufficiently, keep the arm beside the body rather than swinging it behind the hips. Reduce excessive changes in body height.

Your center of gravity remains too high. Bend your knees more and maintain your weight over the forefeet. Lower the wrist and avoid flicking it excessively. Coordinate the upper-body weight movement with the shoulder and arm so that they do not act separately.
Your center of gravity rises too much, making the action look like a jump. Keep it more stable and reduce the large fluctuations, which interfere with preparation for the next stroke.

Your center of gravity is still too high, and the chest and waist remain too upright. Soften the chest and draw in the abdomen. Complete the forearm movement more fully, lower the wrist, and stabilize its loose angle.

Your readiness to initiate movement is encouraging, but you become hesitant and start too late. Step in with the ball's rhythm instead of making repeated waiting movements. Keep the wrist farther from the body, approximately two or three fist-widths away. Brushing the lower part of the ball is good, but the contact is too soft; add a brief burst of force. Start earlier and contact farther forward to use the incoming ball's momentum.

The push is generally good, but avoid excessive wrist flicking. Lower the wrist into an approximately straight, 180-degree alignment with the forearm. Contact is too late and the racket face too flat, producing a high arc. Make the racket more upright, around 45 degrees, to improve trajectory control.

Your rhythm has improved, and you wait for the ball more appropriately. However, wrist force remains insufficient: the backswing is present, but the brief downward cutting action is missing. The left shoulder opens too far outward. Lean the chest slightly forward to control the ball rather than opening the upper body.

Your center of gravity is too high, contact is late, and the wrist is loose. Use the forearm and wrist rather than driving the push with the upper arm. Keep the wrist stable and control shoulder alignment during contact.

Avoid tilting the shoulders to produce the push, particularly dropping the right shoulder. Keep the body leaning and the weight pressing forward instead. Wrist movement is reasonably good, but it still lacks a brief explosive application of force.

Your push is generally good, and weight control has improved. Make the upper-arm and forearm movements smaller, stabilize the wrist, and let the forearm drive the stroke rather than the wrist. Contact is still slightly late.
Your action is good, but contact occurs too late and too close to the body, leaving little room for an explosive application of force. Rotate your waist more.

The overall action, force application, and weight control are good. For topspin, draw the forearm backward rather than downward during preparation. The wrist turns inward slightly; align it with the forearm at approximately 180 degrees and turn it slightly outward at contact.

You are beginning to move your weight with a good sense of rhythm, but the early strokes show too much swaying, which disrupts contact timing and positioning. The forearm remains stiff, and the wrist lacks a brief burst of force. Relax the forearm and rotate the waist more to contribute additional force. Your lowered posture and controlled shoulder movement are good.

The overall action and weight control are good. Open the backswing angle to approximately 180 degrees rather than keeping it smaller. Contact the ball earlier and open the upper-arm action more when applying force.
You miss the intended contact timing, and the forearm remains too tense. Relax the upper arm more as well.

The overall movement has no major problem, and weight control is good. Refine the wrist angle during the backswing so that it aligns with the forearm or extends slightly beyond that alignment. Contact is too late, causing you to miss the best opportunity to apply force.

Your brief explosive force and contact with the lower side of the ball are good, as is the step-in movement. However, the arm rhythm and contact timing do not match the incoming ball, leaving you rushed and sometimes unable to meet it.

Your center of gravity is too high, with an upright waist and insufficient knee bend. Keep the upper arm closer to the body during the forehand push, with the angle below 90 degrees and preferably below 45 degrees. Lower the raised wrist and let the forearm drive the stroke rather than the wrist. The racket face is too upright; flatten it.

Footwork and forward weight orientation have improved, and the shoulders press forward well. However, you rush contact without leaving enough backswing or brushing time. While learning the rhythm, keep the left foot planted and step in with the right rather than moving both feet. Draw the hand backward as you step in, then cut down at contact to brush the lower part of the ball.

Your center of gravity is slightly better but remains too high. Bend the knees more, lean forward at the waist, and keep weight over the forefeet. The wrist is raised too high; maintain a straight wrist-to-forearm alignment when viewed from the side. Contact earlier, near the rising side of the bounce before the peak, and drive the stroke mainly with the forearm rather than the wrist.

Your preparation is too short and begins too late, leaving insufficient forearm backswing. Draw the forearm farther backward and establish the flatter racket angle needed to brush the lower part of the ball.

Your lower-body posture is lower, but the upper body does not lean forward, so your weight remains too far back. The wrist is stiff, and the racket face too upright; flatten the face and keep the shoulder and upper arm closer to the body. Overall, there has been improvement.

The tightening action and force-producing posture are good, and the waist and arm now move together. However, the core remains unstable, causing swaying; stand more firmly and engage the core. The shoulder still works too hard, so waist force does not fully reach the arm and the movement appears stiff.

Your center of gravity is too high, especially in the upper body. Lean forward, bend the knees, and keep weight over the forefeet. The forearm backswing drops below table height; draw it backward above the table instead. Lower the excessively raised wrist toward alignment with the forearm. Complete the upper-body movement and coordinate shoulder, trunk, and leg force more effectively.

Stand more firmly and engage your core. The contact point is too low and close to the thigh; position it diagonally forward at roughly 40 degrees rather than close to the body. You use too much leg force. Reduce it and coordinate more shoulder and arm contribution.

Your overall movement, weight control, and waist and hip rotation have improved. Still, lean the upper body farther forward and bend the knees more. Keep the forearm backswing above the table rather than below it, and lower the raised wrist at contact. Make the racket face approximately 10 to 15 degrees more upright for better contact.
Relax before contact and feel the forearm applying force through the stroke. Avoid a stiff action driven by the upper arm.

Wrist movement is insufficient; use more of its brief explosive force. Your positioning for the ball is inaccurate, so step in faster and locate the contact point more precisely. Avoid large fluctuations in your center of gravity.

Shoulder movement and forearm force application have improved. The main remaining issues are weight control and footwork. Step diagonally forward and right into the table rather than directly sideways. Lean your upper body forward into the table and keep the shoulder closer to the body.

Press diagonally forward rather than directly right when moving in. Reach forward more while drawing the wrist farther backward during preparation. Use more wrist force in the brief forward action, and avoid pressing the shoulder downward excessively.
Shift your upper-body weight forward, relax the wrist, and keep the movement stable while applying force with the forearm.
You press the right shoulder downward too much.

Your lower-body posture is too high and unstable. Bend the right knee forward and feel the right leg pushing against the ground before contact instead of leaving weight too far left. Reduce upward wrist flicking and direct force forward, feeling the right index finger press forward. A later note says the knees and waist are already sufficiently bent despite the high center of gravity.
review_notes: The coach gives differing assessments of knee and waist bend within this summary; the relevant moments are unspecified.

comment_en: The forearm and wrist movement range has improved, but waist rotation is still absent and weight remains on the left foot. Rotate farther right and place more weight over the right leg. After hitting, lean forward rather than sitting backward. The wrist also flicks too much; keep it firmer.

The left foot moves excessively, disrupting both balance and footwork. Feel the toes gripping the ground before contact. Your waist is too upright and weight shifts toward the heels; lean forward to load the forefeet. Direct force forward instead of predominantly upward.

Your racket-swing range is good, but weight still favors the left side and you sit backward after contact. Maintain a forward lean after hitting and make the rightward waist rotation before contact more pronounced.

Your posture is too upright. Bend the right knee farther forward, feel the right toes gripping the ground, and lean your upper body farther into the table. Keep the shoulder closer to the body so that contact is controlled by the body rather than the shoulder alone. Stabilize the wrist, use the forearm to strike, and grip the racket firmly with the fingers instead of resting them loosely on it.
Your upper-arm and forearm movements are too large. Reduce the forearm range, avoid swinging the upper arm backward, and simply press the forearm forward. Contact the ball slightly earlier.
You have found a better feeling of keeping the arm close to the body. Strike with the forearm rather than leading with the upper arm. Control the left hand before contact and direct force forward.
review_notes: Placeholder text and an unclear final directional fragment were omitted or reduced to their intelligible content.

comment_en: Make the movement smaller and contact the ball farther forward. The upper body sways too much; establish a firm stance and keep it stable. When stepping in, let your body move forward with the foot instead of swaying sideways.

Waist rotation and the backward racket preparation have improved, but the hips remain stiff and do not rotate. Your posture is too high; keep the knees bent before and after contact. The index finger sits away from the racket rubber, showing that the fingers are not gripping firmly. Use a secure finger grip rather than relying on wrist force alone. Include hip rotation and weight transfer instead of producing the stroke mainly with the shoulder.

Your body sways too much; stabilize your weight. Increase rightward waist rotation during preparation, as the current range is too small to build force before contact. Finish in front of your nose rather than drawing the arm across to the left shoulder.

Grip the racket firmly with the palm and fingers rather than holding it loosely. At contact, feel the right index fingertip pressing the racket forward and slightly left. Your weight is too far back, and the coach also asks for a backward racket preparation.

Make the backward racket preparation and waist rotation more pronounced; the shoulder currently sinks during this movement. Finish with a controlled closing action in front rather than carrying it to the left shoulder. Avoid side-to-side upper-body sway and establish stable weight support.

Your center of gravity is too high. Step the right foot forward into the table and lean forward at the waist. You use too much wrist force; stabilize the wrist in a straight, approximately 180-degree alignment with the forearm and let the forearm lead the stroke.

You do not use a step-in movement, and the wrist turns too much in a circular brushing action. Use a short downward wrist action with a clearer burst of force instead. Step forward with the right foot to press toward the ball, and keep the left hand beside your body rather than on your waist.

Your center of gravity is too high. Bend the knees forward toward the table and step the right foot farther into the table. Reduce excessive wrist movement, keep the wrist stable, and feel the forearm applying the force.
review_notes: The Chinese field contains corrupted text; the readable English fields were used.

comment_en: The wrist follows a circular path. Replace it with a direct diagonal downward movement and return. Add a step-in action and raise the right shoulder from its overly lowered position.

Your center of gravity remains too high. Step the right foot farther into the table and shift weight toward it, feeling the toes gripping the ground. Avoid a semicircular wrist action. Keep the wrist stable and apply a cleaner downward force driven by the forearm.

Wrist movement is too large, and contact occurs too far back. Use a brief, more explosive wrist action. After contact, stabilize the racket rather than tracing an upward circle, then recover and perform the next downward action.

Your backward racket preparation has increased, but right-knee bend remains insufficient. Bend both legs more, allowing the right knee to turn slightly right, and lower the right shoulder a little. Raise the forearm into a backward backswing rather than letting it drop naturally downward. Lean your weight forward over the forefeet.

Contact timing makes the movement awkward; improve your footwork. Reduce excessive upper-body sway and the large movement range of both shoulders. Rotate the waist more and develop a brief burst of force at contact, with an appropriate transition between tension and release in the forearm.

Your center of gravity is too high, especially on the right side. The waist and hips do not lead the movement, leaving the shoulder to perform the stroke alone. Let the waist and hips carry the whole upper body forward rather than using the hand to pull the waist around.
Both your upper and lower body sway too much during the movement.

Your rhythm is disorganized, and the action resembles a large chop. Move your feet forward to meet the ball and make the stroke smaller. Contact farther forward instead of letting the ball travel behind you. The forearm range is reasonably good but can be reduced slightly; use more wrist force to brush the underside of the ball with a downward cut.

The overall movement is too large, and weight does not shift forward and right. The wrist is raised too high, while the backswing dominates the action. Shorten backward preparation and emphasize the forward movement through and after contact.

Your shoulders sink too much. Contact is acceptably early at first but becomes later as the round progresses. Remove unnecessary movement, draw the arm slightly backward, and use a brief wrist action to brush the ball. Avoid a large chopping stroke; lean forward to meet the ball while keeping the shoulders steady.
Your wrist stability has improved.
review_notes: The isolated phrase about left-right transition gives no clear assessment or instruction and was omitted.

comment_en: Your racket now stays farther forward, and you move forward to the ball, which is good. Strengthen the wrist action and keep the racket face flatter to lower the trajectory. Find the ball with your body rather than the shoulder alone, bringing both shoulders slightly forward.

You have improved considerably, particularly in weight control and contact positioning. Contact the ball on the upper-right area of the racket rather than the left or lower-left area. Lean your upper body farther forward and make the action smaller.
Your feet remain fixed, leaving the ball too close to the right hip. Move slightly left to create space and rotate your waist farther to the right.
Your force application is connected and explosive. Lower the right shoulder a little more; an overly small joint angle makes the action stiff.

Your brief force application is good, but footwork and waist rotation remain insufficient. Move the feet farther left to create room and time for the complete stroke, and rotate the waist more. Load the right foot before contact and return weight toward the middle afterward rather than beginning in the middle and shifting too far left.

Shoulder movement has improved, but weight transfer goes too far left. Control the movement forward first and then left, rather than moving directly left and losing force on the ball. Lean the action forward, bring the hips forward, and lower the right knee slightly more.

Your force application is good, but the shoulder is stiff. Your position is acceptable without being fully comfortable; adjust slightly left to find the ball. Keep your weight leaning forward after contact. The backswing is too short, so recover immediately after each stroke and prepare the next backswing promptly.

Your movement directs too much force upward and too little forward, especially through the shoulder. The shoulder is held too high; let the right shoulder settle naturally. Direct force forward rather than left, and lean the upper body farther forward because the waist remains too high.

Your forearm-closing action is good, but you substitute dropping the shoulder for waist rotation. Keep the shoulders more level and rotate the waist horizontally to the right. Place more weight over the right foot and combine this rotation with your existing forearm action to improve backswing preparation.

Raise the forearm during the backswing instead of dropping it downward. Increase backward waist rotation. Your center of gravity is slightly high, so bend your knees more and lean forward. Raise the left hand to maintain balance between both sides.
Your contact timing and sense of rhythm are very good. Turn to the right, relax the wrist slightly, and avoid excessive wrist flicking.

The overall action has improved substantially, especially weight transfer. Raise the left hand to maintain balance. Stabilize the racket through the index finger and thumb rather than relying on a large wrist action.

You hesitate and do not accelerate enough; apply force more decisively at contact. Reduce excessive shoulder movement and let the waist lead the arm, with weight over the right foot. Finishing in front of the nose and the current contact point are both acceptable.

Lower your center of gravity further and combine body and shoulder force more effectively. Focus on transferring force from the feet through the waist and shoulder to the wrist, rather than merely reproducing the appearance of a standard action.
Maintain a consistent wrist position throughout the block.

The overall action is good, but bend the knees more. Adjust the grip so that the index finger sits more closely against the racket face without a gap. Rotate the racket slightly toward the index finger to transfer its force to the ball more effectively.

Your movement is too large for the block. Reduce forearm travel, keep the action compact, and use the incoming ball's momentum. Keep your feet steady, making a small adjustment and planting firmly when needed. The wrist is raised and the racket wobbles; secure the grip and tilt the racket slightly forward rather than backward.

Your center of gravity remains too high. Bend the knees farther forward and feel the forefeet supporting your weight. Adjust the grip so that the index finger fits closely against the racket face without a gap, and raise the angle formed by the hand web and racket handle slightly.

Your shoulders are tense and the movement is not relaxed enough. Make the action more compact, reduce its excessive range, and improve balance and foot stability. Adjust the wrist position and keep the action consistent.
Your knees do not bend enough. An incorrect grip causes the racket to tilt too far backward toward your body during contact. Adjust it approximately 15 degrees forward.

Your whole body is stiff, and the step-in foot is planted too rigidly. Do not place all your weight on the right forefoot. Prepare earlier, step into a stable position, and allow a brief moment before contact rather than striking immediately upon stepping. Relax the shoulders, reduce forearm dominance, and use more wrist action to brush the ball.

Weight adjustment is too slow. Prepare the right foot forward and step it into the table earlier, while leaning the upper body farther forward. The stroke is too large. Let the forearm and wrist lead the upper arm rather than using the upper arm and forearm to drag the wrist through contact.

Step-in timing improves later in the round. Keep a measured rhythm instead of rushing the step. Reduce the oversized forearm action and use more wrist force to brush the ball rather than lifting it forcefully with the forearm. Open the wrist slightly outward instead of folding it inward, and relax the shoulder rather than using it to generate force.

Use the fingers to apply force, especially the tip of the index finger rather than its pad. The overall action is too large; keep the forearm and upper arm controlled in front and to the right. Let the index finger lead the racket face, followed by the forearm and upper arm through contact.
Keep the stepping action pressing forward. Reduce the forearm's large movement, use more wrist force, relax the shoulder, and contact the ball earlier.

You rely almost entirely on the shoulder and upper arm. For the flick, emphasize wrist and finger force instead. Relax before contact and improve wrist mobility. Press forward with the fingers and wrist rather than the upper arm, which makes the stroke too large and causes the ball to miss the table.

The toss is too low at first but improves later. The forearm remains cramped; open the elbow and draw the forearm farther backward. Continue the action forward after contact instead of finishing upward. Press the forearm forward more.
Increase the backswing and place the ball in the center of the tossing palm.
review_notes: The source alternates between left and right tossing hands; no hand was selected by inference.

comment_en: Finish the serving action by pressing forward rather than drawing the arm upward.
Place the ball in the center of the tossing palm and include waist rotation, which is currently absent.
review_notes: The source refers to both left and right tossing hands without clarifying which is intended.

comment_en: Move the upper arm slightly farther from the torso so that the forearm can travel farther backward during preparation. Keep the racket face flatter to brush the lower part of the ball.
Place the ball in the center of your left palm before tossing it.
Use a stronger brief burst of wrist force.
Your center of gravity is too high during contact. Bend the right knee lower and lean forward more at the waist. Keep the wrist stable rather than loose.

Your stroke moves too much from back to front, sending the ball high. Use a more downward cutting action or a more upright racket face. Step-in timing varies; locate the ball and step into position more consistently. Reduce excessive forearm movement and increase wrist force.
Do not let the right knee turn outward. Apply force with all the fingers, make the right wrist action more apparent, and avoid bending the wrist inward.

Your racket moves upward after contact, sending the ball too high. Use more downward wrist force through the finish. Step in earlier and advance the contact timing, which becomes progressively later during the round.

Bend your knees more to improve your lower-body posture. Stabilize the wrist and racket face during contact, and let the forearm apply force with support from the fingers rather than allowing the wrist to loosen.

You appear less comfortable at first, but the movement becomes smaller and more controlled later. Raise the hand slightly and briefly secure the racket at contact to absorb the incoming ball's force. Step in earlier and improve the rhythm. Your shoulders sink too far; raise them slightly and keep them more level.
The racket face is too upright; flatten it. Lean your weight forward, bend the right knee farther forward, and incline your upper body at the waist.
Avoid turning the wrist over during the stroke.

Your center of gravity remains too high, and the wrist is too loose at contact. Keep the wrist aligned with the forearm at approximately 180 degrees and use the forearm to control the ball rather than applying force with the wrist. Contact just after the bounce instead of waiting for the highest point.

Your contact point is too far back; keep it farther forward. Raise the forearm and racket slightly. As you secure the grip, use a clear downward wrist action at contact, then release the incoming force after contact to control the return.
Your racket grip is incorrect and needs adjustment.

Your brief explosive force is good, but the follow-through is too large. Stop in front of the nose or slightly earlier instead of finishing near the ear or above the head. Relax the shoulder and avoid lifting it to generate force. Make the contribution from waist rotation more pronounced.

You use the upper arm too much, making the whole action oversized. Let the waist rotate backward first and carry the shoulder and arm into preparation, rather than drawing the arms back independently. After contact, control the upper arm instead of pushing it too far forward, and reduce the angle between it and the body.

Your wrist tilts backward, and the shoulder works too hard, carrying the arm above the head. Relax the shoulder and combine waist rotation with forearm closing. Increase actual waist rotation rather than merely pressing downward. Keep weight forward and controlled after contact instead of rising upward or sitting backward.

Your backswing drops below the table. Raise the forearm and draw it backward rather than downward. The upper arm travels too far forward after contact, making the finish large and uncontrolled. Reduce the angle between the upper arm and body.

Use waist rotation more clearly instead of lifting with the upper arm and right shoulder. The forearm-closing action and explosive force are very good, but the finish passes the nose and reaches above the head. Keep it more compact and avoid excessive effort. Maintain weight forward after contact rather than falling backward.

The overall action has improved slightly. Raise the forearm, reduce excessive right-shoulder effort, and let the shoulder settle and relax during contact. Control the angle between the upper arm and body.
Use a more distinct burst of wrist force to brush the ball, and contact it farther forward.

Your movement is too large. Apply force with the forearm rather than the shoulder and upper arm. Lower the slightly raised wrist and keep the racket aligned with the forearm at approximately 180 degrees. Lean your weight forward and stabilize the wrist as the forearm meets the ball.
Bring the wrist farther forward and open it slightly outward. Increase the contribution of the wrist and forearm to the stroke.

Your weight orientation has improved with a greater forward lean, but the backswing is excessive and the action retracts as soon as contact occurs. Continue farther forward through and after contact to complete the stroke. Contact is too far back; meet the ball near its highest point or slightly earlier.
Prepare the racket diagonally in front of the body and move forward from there. Avoid folding the wrist inward; open it slightly outward and use wrist force to cut the ball. Contact a little earlier.
Your weight control has improved, but the backswing remains too large. Move the action farther forward and increase the forward continuation after contact instead of emphasizing backward preparation.
Your overall action is good. Relax the right shoulder and let it move with the body. After contact, avoid sitting backward; keep a slight forward lean with weight over both forefeet.

Feel the toes and forefeet gripping the ground, bend the knees more, and lean the upper body farther forward. You finish with weight over the heels, particularly on the left side. Relax the upper body and apply force from a less rigid posture.
Relax the shoulders and contact the ball earlier; your current timing is too late.

The backswing has changed slightly but still needs adjustment. Keep the upper arm closer to the body during preparation. Your weight tends to move backward after contact; press the upper body forward through the strike, as though controlling the ball from above.

Your forearm and wrist are too stiff. Relax the wrist, initiate the stroke earlier, and prepare the backswing sooner to allow enough time. Your feet are not moving and need to contribute to positioning.

Keep the racket and forearm aligned at approximately 180 degrees when viewed from the side rather than bending the angle above or below that alignment. Your center of gravity is too high; bend the knees and lean forward at the waist. The contact point itself is good.

The stroke lacks a brief burst of force, a clear step-in action, and forward weight movement. After drawing the wrist back, bring it forward decisively rather than leaving it behind. Use the racket face to brush the lower part of the ball, and relax the shoulder and forearm.

Your weight is not over the forefeet, and the upper body is too high, leaving the hand too far from the body. Lean forward, reduce the upper-arm-to-body angle, and keep the wrist aligned with the forearm at approximately 180 degrees. Drive the push with the forearm rather than the wrist.
Your forward weight orientation has improved, which is positive. However, wrist force remains insufficient, and the feet still do not make a clear forward step.

Wrist-to-forearm alignment and contact positioning have improved, allowing better control and brushing. Weight control is also slightly better, but lean the upper body farther forward and bring the elbow closer to the body. The wrist is still overly extended. Reduce upper-arm force and use the forearm while maintaining a stable wrist angle.

Your wrist bends too far backward, making the stroke look like a push. Bring it forward so that the racket and forearm form a straighter line. Waist rotation is absent, and the upper arm and shoulder are stiff. Relax them, make the forearm-closing action more distinct, and add waist rotation.

The overall movement is good, but the wrist is too loose during contact. Your upper-body weight is too high; bend the knees slightly more and lean forward. Combine waist and hip force with the shoulder instead of relying only on the hand.

Waist and hip rotation are delayed and separated; coordinate them to transfer force to the hand promptly. The wrist still bends backward, so press it slightly forward. If the incoming ball is backspin, as the coach suspects, add more brushing contact rather than relying mainly on impact.

Your center of gravity remains high but has improved. Force application is stronger, and the waist and hips now contribute. Lower the raised wrist into an approximately straight, 180-degree alignment with the forearm for better force transmission.

Your wrist remains bent backward, making it difficult to transfer force to the ball. Press it slightly forward so the racket faces more toward the table. Relax the stiff shoulder and arms, complete waist rotation and forearm closing more fully, and allow more time for the backswing.

Your overall force application has improved, but a stiff wrist leaves the upper arm doing most of the work and prevents effective forearm force, contributing to missed balls. Lower the wrist and feel the fingers leading the racket face through contact. Your posture is better but still high; bend the knees more to transfer lower-body force through the waist and hips into the upper body.
Your body sways continuously, disrupting rhythm and making stroke initiation inconsistent. The wrist is too stiff. Relax it between strokes and tighten the grip briefly at contact.

Your center of gravity is too high, and the racket is too far from your body. The wrist is loose, while the upper arm rather than the forearm drives contact. Stabilize the wrist and forearm in an approximately straight alignment and contact the ball on the upper-right area of the racket rather than the lower-left area.

Wrist action and body stability have improved. Still, use a clearer downward wrist cut and a brief burst of force. Initiate the stroke earlier and contact farther forward, as the contact point remains too far back.

Brushing contact has improved, but the wrist still flicks excessively. Bend the knees and lean the upper body forward to lower your high center of gravity. Keep the wrist aligned with the forearm at approximately 180 degrees and use the upper-right or central racket area, rather than the lower-left area caused by excessive wrist movement.

Your contact point is too far back, and the racket face is too upright, causing impact rather than brushing. Flatten the face to brush the lower part of the ball. Wrist action is present but needs a fuller preparation and forward continuation. Bring the shoulder inward and forward rather than leaving it back and outward.
review_notes: The source gives inconsistent or unclear 80-to-90-degree wrist-range wording; no precise angle was inferred.

comment_en: Your weight control has improved but remains too high. The racket angle is too flat during contact. Remove unnecessary movements so that you can prepare for the next stroke in time. Brushing timing is better in this round.
Begin preparation earlier to allow sufficient backswing. After contact, stop the movement cleanly rather than continuing along an unnecessarily long follow-through path.

The overall action is good, but your center of gravity is too high. The upper arm finishes too close to the body; leave some space between them. Improve the connection between lower and upper body, as the high posture leaves the shoulder supplying most of the force.

Recovery is too slow. Finish promptly and avoid holding the racket near the head for too long. Relax the shoulder after recovery. Allow more preparation time and a longer backswing, then stop cleanly after contact.
review_notes: A final fragment about reducing movement length is unclear about the phase and was not used to override the explicit longer-backswing instruction.

comment_en: Your weight control has improved, particularly in the upper body, and the lower right shoulder helps force application. However, the racket-to-forearm angle exceeds 180 degrees during preparation; keep it aligned at approximately 180 degrees at contact. Lower the lower-body posture further by bending the knees more.

Your rhythm is very good, but the shoulder is stiff, leaving the shoulder and arm to supply most of the force. Relax it and increase coordinated waist rotation to transfer force to the hand. Avoid bending the wrist backward; press it and the racket face slightly forward to brush the side of the ball.

The overall stroke and force application have improved. Prepare backward waist rotation before contact, then strike as the force moves forward rather than rotating only after hitting. Keep the rotation within a controlled range. Reduce wrist flicking and bend the knees more to lower the lower-body posture.

Your action becomes very stiff after contact. Keep a secure racket grip without straightening and locking the forearm; the arm should remain bent. Contact earlier and farther forward. Tilt the racket face slightly backward to brush the lower part of the ball.

Both upper- and lower-body posture are too high. Keep weight over the forefeet and lean forward. Bring the upper arm closer to the body and reduce its force contribution, using the forearm for the push instead. The racket-to-forearm angle and contact timing are good.

Contact farther forward and use more wrist force rather than relying on the forearm. Relax the shoulder and lean your body forward to meet the ball. Do not find the ball with the hand alone or let the hand move too far from the body.

Your upper-body posture is too high. Keep the upper arm closer to the body and the racket in front, within a smaller distance from the torso. Reduce excessive upper-arm force and use the forearm. Coordinate shoulder and body force so that both act on the ball together.

You now produce a downward cutting action, but flatten the racket face further to increase brushing contact. The shoulder tends to press downward. Lean the whole body forward rather than using the shoulder alone to press toward the ball.

Your body position has improved with a slight forward lean, but more is needed. The racket remains too far from the body; keep the action within a smaller range and avoid unnecessarily carrying the upper arm with the forearm. Reduce the oversized racket-face angle toward approximately 45 degrees at contact.

You use the wrist mainly to hit the ball. Tilt the racket face farther forward and brush the side of the ball more. Begin preparation earlier to allow a longer backswing. Stop cleanly after contact instead of continuing through an excessively long recovery path.

Your center of gravity is too high and is not supported over the forefeet. Bend the knees and lean forward. You become tense before contact, making force application stiff. Relax the wrist and forearm instead of keeping them rigid. Your contact point is well controlled.

The later strokes show good brushing contact, whereas the early strokes rely more on impact with an overly turned wrist. Increase backswing distance and preparation time, relax the shoulder, and rotate the waist a little more.

Waist and hip rotation have improved significantly, combining with the arm to produce more force. Lower your lower-body posture, keep weight over the forefeet, and lean forward. Leave approximately 5 to 10 centimeters more space between the upper arm and body. Lower the wrist and reduce excessive outward racket rotation, keeping the racket and forearm aligned at approximately 180 degrees during contact.

Your arm action and brushing contact are good, but the backswing remains too short. The legs are stiff; bend them slightly more to lower your weight. Complete waist rotation more fully and draw the hand backward with the waist so that both rotation and backswing have sufficient range.

Force application has improved greatly, with better waist and hip contribution. However, your posture remains too high, especially in the lower body, and the knees do not bend enough. You still rely mainly on upper-body force. Lower your weight over the forefeet to connect the whole movement more effectively.

Your rhythm, stepping, and forward weight transfer are good. The forearm does not draw back far enough, and the wrist lacks a brief burst of force, leaving the ball slow. Use a sharper wrist action to cut down and brush the lower part of the ball for more spin.

The overall action and contact timing are good, but your lower-body posture is too high, leaving too much distance between the body and racket. Bend the right knee more. The racket is raised too high, causing contact on its lower-left area. Use the upper-right or upper-right central area instead.

Wrist force and forearm movement are more pronounced, but your feet remain fixed, making some contacts awkward. Move your feet to find the ball rather than staying in one place. Apply wrist force more decisively in a brief burst, meet the ball farther forward, and bring your body forward with it.

Your center of gravity remains too high. Shorten the backswing and return to a position near the contact point instead of pulling far backward while waiting. Lower the raised wrist and bring the racket closer to the body. Step the right foot slightly forward and bend the right knee more, using the body rather than the hand alone to control the push.

Contact is too late, and you reach for the ball without moving your feet forward. The right shoulder moves too much. Reduce shoulder and backward arm movement, lean the whole body forward, and use a brief wrist action to cut the lower part of the ball.

Your weight control has improved, but place the right foot farther forward and bend the right knee more. The backswing while waiting is too large. Prepare closer to the stroke's starting position and allow more forward movement through contact, as the current action leaves too little time to brush the ball.

Waist rotation, leg drive, and the brief force during forearm closing are very good. However, the shoulder is stiff and the wrist shakes, disrupting contact timing. Turn the wrist slightly inward and stabilize it, with the racket face inclined forward to brush the side of the ball.

The overall action and coordination of waist, hips, and upper body are good. Lean your upper-body weight farther forward. The racket turns too far outward at contact; keep it aligned with the forearm at approximately 180 degrees rather than beyond that angle.

The wrist turns outward excessively, and the hand travels behind the waist, making the action too large. Lean the trunk forward and finish with the forearm in front of the eyes. Coordinate waist rotation and forearm closing more compactly instead of separating them.

The racket backswing is too large relative to waist rotation, making force application poorly coordinated. Lean the upper body farther forward. Rotate the waist and shoulder forward together, allowing the waist to lead the shoulder rather than preparing with the forearm alone or using the shoulder to pull the waist.

Excessive foot movement makes your weight sway. Stabilize your stance and maintain a forward lean after contact. Meet the ball farther in front instead of letting it fall beside the body. Rotate the waist and close the forearm together, keeping the hand from lagging behind the waist, and avoid excessive wrist tilting.

Waist force is good, but the forehand backswing remains too large. Let waist rotation organize the backswing instead of throwing the arm around. Limit outward wrist rotation and keep it aligned with the forearm at approximately 180 degrees. Make the overall action smaller.

Your lower-body posture is too high. Bend the knees, lean forward at the waist, and keep weight over the forefeet. The backswing travels too far to the right, leaving the upper arm too far from the body. Bring it closer and coordinate shoulder and body force.

You rely mainly on the arm without combining it with waist force. The shoulder works too hard and appears braced. Relax it so that it connects the waist and arm rather than adding excessive effort. Increase waist rotation and its force contribution, and close the forearm faster at contact.

Bend your knees more and increase waist and hip rotation backward and to the right. Keep the upper arm closer to the body during contact. Raise the left hand rather than letting it hang beside you, maintaining balance between both sides.

Increase the backward preparation range of both the waist and forearm. Waist rotation and forearm closing do not yet combine their force effectively. Coordinate waist and wrist force so that they act together in a brief burst.

Feel the index fingertip pressing forward to apply force rather than using its pad or joint. Keep the upper arm closer to the body during contact, and raise the left hand to maintain balance between both sides.
Use a clearer diagonal recovery and preparation path after each stroke. Make the action cleaner and more direct, and increase backswing distance slightly.

The overall contact action is good, but lower your weight and lean forward more. Keep the upper arm closer to the body and reduce the angle between the upper arm and forearm. Raising the forearm slightly during preparation should help.

Your use of the incoming ball's force is good. Let the ball rise slightly and meet it a little farther back. Relax the shoulders, thighs, and wrist, and use a gentle forearm-closing action to redirect the incoming force.
review_notes: The Chinese requests a farther-back contact point, while the English reverses that instruction. The merged text follows the Chinese.

comment_en: Bend your knees more, especially the right knee. The stroke is incomplete and lacks active upper-arm contribution. Combine it with the forearm and complete the movement toward the left eyebrow. Rotate the waist more and feel the waist and hips leading the shoulder through contact.
Your overall action is excellent. Allow the ball to rise slightly higher, relax the shoulders and wrist more, and use a controlled forearm-closing movement.

Shift your weight farther forward into the table and step the right foot another half-step forward. The wrist is too tight; relax it and use more wrist-led force rather than fixing the wrist and forearm together. Draw the racket back with the right index finger, then press forward with its tip as you strike. Relax the wrist again after contact.

Allow the ball to rise a little more. Avoid bending or flicking the wrist backward; hold it slightly forward and close the forearm. Relax the shoulder and wrist, using the forearm to redirect the incoming ball's force. Your weight sways noticeably early in the round but improves later. Engage the core to keep the upper body from moving side to side.

Shift lower-body weight slightly right and step the right foot half a step farther forward. Relax the wrist before contact, open it backward, and then strike forward. The wrist is currently too fixed, causing excessive forearm effort; allow a more relaxed wrist action.

Variations in ball speed make receiving difficult, and the shoulder remains stiff. Contact is too far forward; allow the ball to rise a little more and use its incoming force. Relax the shoulder and wrist, and use waist rotation during preparation instead of drawing the racket back with the hand alone.

You are still not relaxed enough, and active backward preparation is too small. Draw the wrist back more deliberately, then press the right index fingertip against the racket as you strike forward. Shift weight forward and right, step the right foot another half-step forward, and lean the upper body farther into the table.
Avoid swinging the wrist backward.

Weight transfer is incomplete. After serving, move weight onto the left leg rather than leaving it on the right, adding a clear left-foot landing. A higher toss could provide more time for the backswing and help coordinate whole-body force as the ball descends, improving serve speed and quality.
The upper arm is held too tightly against the torso, and the forearm, wrist, and shoulder are too tense. Relax these areas and avoid clamping the arm in place.
Increase the range of the backward racket preparation.
The wrist begins moving too early; delay its action.
Bend the right knee more. Avoid a large swinging forearm action or unnecessarily complicated movement. Keep the force directed forward and to the right.
Make the wrist's force contribution more pronounced.

Because the right foot does not step far enough forward, the upper body leans excessively into the table. Step in farther and balance upper- and lower-body weight. Wrist stability has improved, but the stroke still feels like a downward scrape. Shorten the backswing and direct the smaller action forward rather than scraping downward.
The wrist's brief explosive force is not pronounced enough.

Step the right foot farther into the table and balance upper- and lower-body weight. Keep the wrist stable rather than loose and feel the forearm applying force. Raise the left hand instead of leaving it beside or behind your body.
Make the brief explosive force more pronounced. Since the ball is short, step farther forward and lean the body forward to find the contact point. Meet the ball slightly farther in front.
Step farther forward into the table with the right foot. Keep the wrist stable during contact and feel the forearm applying force.

The short-touch action may be too small; increase it slightly. Prepare the racket upward, then use a small downward cut. Control improves in the latter part of the round. Add a step-in action and a forward-weight-then-recovery movement instead of remaining fixed in place.

The racket face is too upright; tilt it back into a flatter position. Contact earlier, just after the bounce, and continue the contact action long enough to brush the ball. Move the right leg and your weight farther forward.

The preparation range is insufficient and mainly backward. Raise the forearm more during preparation, then use a small downward press on the ball. A step-in action is now present, but combine it with a clear recovery afterward.

Your contact point is well controlled, but the contact action is too brief to brush the ball effectively, producing a high arc. Flatten the racket face and make the downward-forward forearm action slightly fuller. Do not stop immediately upon touching the ball; complete the action to improve brushing and trajectory control.

Use less wrist action for the short touch and let the forearm press downward. Add a clear step-in and recovery sequence. You currently stand too rigidly in one place; move weight forward into contact and then recover.

The shoulder appears to lead the entire stroke. Keep the upper arm closer to the body and let the waist and hips lead both arms instead of using the hand to pull the waist. Lower your weight, bend the knees more, and feel the whole body applying force together rather than focusing on the shoulder.

Rightward waist rotation is too small, while the finish turns too far left. Finish facing the table and increase the rightward preparation, allowing a larger forearm backswing. The brief force during forearm closing is good, but waist force does not fully reach the racket; coordinate both contributions.

The backward preparation is insufficient. Let the hips and waist lead the upper arm backward rather than letting the arm pull the waist around. Keep the overall action tighter and the upper arm closer to the body to coordinate trunk and shoulder force.

Your forearm produces a good brief burst of force, but waist force does not yet transfer effectively to the hand. Use more waist contribution and coordinate waist rotation with forearm closing. Avoid throwing the shoulder backward or letting the hand lag behind the waist.

Lower your center of gravity by bending the knees and waist more. Reduce both the elbow angle and the angle between the upper arm and body, keeping the arm closer in during contact. This should help combine waist and shoulder force on the ball.

Waist rotation is beginning to appear, and more balls land on the table than in the previous round. Increase waist contribution and reduce reliance on the hand. Avoid turning the racket upward while closing the forearm; incline it slightly forward and press your weight forward after contact to keep the ball from flying upward.

The main issue is lower-body weight transfer. Shift slightly toward the right leg before contact and transfer toward the left afterward; you currently remain on the right after hitting. Keep the upper arm slightly closer to the body.

Stabilize your weight and maintain a forward press after contact instead of swaying sideways. Add waist rotation and increase the forearm's backward and rightward preparation range, which is currently too small.
Keep the force-producing action closer to your body to improve control of the ball.
Your upper arm and shoulder are stiff and need to relax. The forearm-closing movement is too small; complete its brief action more fully.

Your overall movement and weight control have improved. Avoid lifting the wrist during force application; keep it aligned with the forearm at approximately 180 degrees, without exceeding that angle. Feel the index finger pressing forward.

Use the waist to bring the arm through instead of relying on shoulder force. Relax the shoulder and let it settle rather than holding it raised. Contact is too far back; strike near the ball's highest point.

Your lower-body stance is too high. Bend both knees forward and avoid excessively outward-pointing feet, adjusting them slightly inward without becoming pigeon-toed. Reduce the upper-arm backswing and keep the arm closer to the body. Let the waist and hips lead the arms during backward rotation, and make the overall action smaller.

You use an attacking action for the block. Reduce force and movement size, relax, and redirect the incoming ball with a compact forearm-closing action. Shorten the backswing instead of drawing far behind you. The wrist tilts backward; relax it and control it slightly forward.

Point both feet more toward the opponent rather than outward to the sides. Reduce the oversized upper-arm preparation and keep the arm closer to the body. Let waist and hip movement lead the shoulder, and stabilize the wrist.
Your shoulders move too much. Keep their movement controlled and compact.
Avoid pressing the wrist too far downward during the backswing. The coach also calls attention to the right-foot position and racket angle, but the directional wording is inconsistent.
review_notes: The source combines 'parallel to the ground' with 'around 45 degrees' and does not clearly specify the intended foot correction.

comment_en: Take a deep breath, exhale gently, and relax.
review_notes: The source consists almost entirely of repeated breathing cues and blank entries, with no specific stroke-quality assessment.

comment_en: Step the right foot forward into the table and lean the upper body forward. Reduce excessive upper-arm force and the large angles between upper arm, torso, and forearm. Relax the wrist and let it initiate contact, with the forearm and upper arm following rather than driving the stroke independently.

The racket is too far from your body, leaving you reaching awkwardly. Move slightly right and lean forward. Reduce the excessive arm extension and relax the shoulder and forearm. Use more wrist force for the flick. Contact is too far back; meet the ball earlier during its rise after the bounce.

Your weight favors the left side. Stand more centrally, step the right foot into the table, and shift weight toward the right leg. Wrist force has improved, but the upper arm still contributes too much. Let the wrist lead the forearm and upper arm rather than actively driving with the upper arm.
Your contact point is too far back, and the hand is too far from the body. Use more wrist force instead of continually lifting the ball with the forearm or shoulder.

Upper-body weight orientation has improved but remains slightly backward. The upper arm supplies too much force, while the wrist is too tight to contribute. Keep the upper arm closer to the body, relax the wrist into the backswing, and press forward through contact with the index finger supporting the racket. Shift weight forward and right.

Your weight is too far back, the forearm swing is too long, and the shoulder and upper arm are stiff. Relax them, shorten the forearm action, and include the wrist in backward preparation before using a brief wrist burst. Move slightly right and step forward with the right foot while leaning in, keeping the hand closer to the body without straightening the arm excessively. The notes also give opposing descriptions of wrist force, calling it both absent and excessive.
review_notes: Conflicting wrist-force descriptions are retained without inventing different phases.

comment_en: Do not let the toss curve outward away from the body. Increase the upper-arm backswing range.
review_notes: An English fragment also warns against an overly rearward backswing, which is not clearly supported by the Chinese transcription; its intended meaning needs review.

comment_en: You stop the racket immediately after contact. Continue it farther forward toward the table to complete the serving action.

Ball placement in the left palm has improved but needs to be more precisely centered. Increase the forearm backswing range and lower your center of gravity to apply body force more effectively to the ball.

Increase the forearm backswing and continue the arm and racket farther forward after contact to control the ball's trajectory. Let the ball descend to roughly hip height instead of contacting it near the chest. Relax the shoulder slightly.

Place the ball in the palm rather than on the fingers. Raise the forearm slightly and draw the racket backward and sideways instead of letting it drop naturally, using the described figure-eight feeling. Hold the racket more upright, with the racket head oriented as nearly perpendicular to the ground as instructed.

Relax the shoulder, upper arm, and forearm. Increase the backward preparation range and add some wrist action to strike or brush the ball. Continue the wrist forward after contact instead of stopping immediately, so that the ball receives a clearer forward force.
Shift your weight farther forward and right, and bend the right knee more. Reduce excessive backward preparation and emphasize a fuller forward action through and after contact.

Wrist force is not fully expressed; increase its contribution while maintaining the good, relaxed upper-arm and shoulder position. Bring the left foot slightly forward. Right-foot stepping is acceptable, but move the body closer to the hand rather than reaching forward with an overly straight arm.

Contact is too late, sometimes occurring during the ball's descent. For a short touch, meet the ball just after the bounce to improve brushing and spin. Step the right foot farther forward, shift weight forward and right, and bend the right knee more.
Your contact timing is still too late.
Bend the right knee more to stabilize your weight. Contact just after the bounce, where the incoming force can be used effectively, rather than waiting for the ball to descend.
Keep your torso from swaying, hold the right hand closer to the body, and angle the racket face downward.

Shift your weight slightly forward and right, feeling the right forefoot gripping the ground. Reduce the angles between upper arm and torso and between forearm and upper arm. Lean the whole body into the table to control the ball. Contact during the early rise after the bounce rather than during descent, allowing better coordinated brushing contact.

The racket-face angle is good. Raise the forearm more during preparation, then press downward at contact. Relax the shoulder and forearm. Trunk sway is reduced compared with earlier videos; maintain that improvement and keep the core slightly firmer.

Raise the forearm and let the waist and hips lead both arms into preparation instead of letting the arms pull the body around. Make the overall movement smaller to concentrate force. During the backswing, keep the racket at about 45 degrees or more to the ground rather than parallel to it.

Waist force is not reaching the racket. Coordinate the hand and waist so that their force acts together at contact. Your torso sways sideways, and the shoulders move both sideways and vertically. Keep weight forward and the core engaged, using a controlled rightward turn followed by a forward press.

The action remains too large, and the racket face is pressed down too far, reducing the contact area and causing edge hits. Open the racket more during preparation, keeping it around 45 degrees or more to the ground rather than parallel. Close the face as you move forward instead of closing it excessively beforehand. Keep the upper arm closer to the body and concentrate the action.

Maintain forward weight and shoulder orientation after contact. Forearm closing is good, but waist force is not contributing fully; the shoulder and upper arm still dominate. Relax them and let the shoulder connect the movement instead of lifting. Finish in front of the nose or eyes rather than above the head.

The racket is too closed during the backswing because of the grip, reducing the usable contact area. Its edge faces toward the thumb rather than the hand web, leaving a gap beneath the index finger. Align the racket edge with the hand web and fit the index finger closely against the face. Increase the contact area, keep the upper arm closer to the body, and reduce its effort to coordinate body and shoulder force.

Make the action smaller and use more waist force. Relax the shoulders and keep them directed forward after contact instead of lifting or turning them excessively left. Press the core and weight forward rather than sitting back or standing upright. Relax the wrist and avoid gripping too tightly.
