Weight transfer is reasonably good, but keep the torso centered and reduce uncontrolled swaying or rotation.

Contact is too far back. Leave slightly more space between the upper arm and body, secure the racket grip, and relax the shoulder. Bend at the waist and draw in the abdomen. Coordinate waist and hand movement with a rightward turn, a downward backswing, and a forward press. Finish in front of the eyes or nose rather than using shoulder force alone.

Your center of gravity is too high, and both knees need more bend. Weight remains on the left leg throughout; shift slightly right before contact and transfer left afterward. Correct the grip so that the index finger touches the racket face without a gap, and hold the racket more firmly when applying force.
Open the wrist outward so that the upper arm and shoulder can relax as well.

The right knee is too straight to let weight settle over the right leg. Bend it forward and feel force transferring from right to left. Grip the racket firmly at contact rather than leaving it loose, and feel the index fingertip pressing forward.
Your knees are too straight. Step back to give yourself more space.

Your upper-body action is good, but the racket grip is too loose, with a large gap beneath the index finger. Move the grip slightly higher and fit the hand web closer to the handle-face junction. Keep the index finger against the racket to concentrate its force on the ball. Point the feet more toward the opponent rather than outward, bend the knees, and maintain weight over the forefeet.
Take a step backward to improve your position.

Bend your knees. Waist and hip rotation are good, but the grip still leaves too much space between the index finger and racket. Close that gap and feel the index fingertip applying force to the racket at contact.

You stand too upright and need to press your weight forward. The ball crowds your contact position, so step back. Recover immediately after hitting rather than pausing, and prepare the next backswing earlier. Grip the racket firmly without wrist flicking. Relax the shoulder and upper arm, keeping the upper arm controlled instead of lifting it. Maintain weight forward after contact rather than moving backward or upward.

Weight transfer has improved slightly but remains limited by insufficient knee bend. Point the feet more toward the opponent rather than outward. Reduce excessive backward upper-arm action and let forearm opening guide the preparation. Adjust the grip to eliminate the gap beneath the index finger and hold the racket firmly with the palm.
Open the wrist outward so that the upper arm and shoulder can relax.

Step the right foot farther into the table and feel weight over the right forefoot. Bend forward more at the waist. Bring the hand closer to the body by reducing the upper-arm-to-body angle, and feel the wrist striking forward.

Your posture is too upright, and the shoulder and upper arm are stiff. Leave slightly more space beside the upper arm and open the wrist outward rather than inward. The forearm backswing is good, but use more wrist action and incline the racket forward to brush the ball. Stop cleanly after contact. Secure the grip at the hand web and include a clearer step-in and recovery movement while keeping weight forward.

The right foot does not step into the table, and the waist remains too high; lean farther forward. Upper-arm positioning has improved but is still insufficient. Grip the racket firmly and eliminate the gap between the finger and racket face so that it does not loosen during force application.

Incline the racket face forward to increase brushing. Contact is too far back, and the racket movement is too large; shorten it and stop cleanly after hitting. The waist and hand act separately. Bend at the waist, draw in the abdomen, coordinate rotation, and relax the shoulder.

Lean the upper body farther into the table and maintain weight over the right forefoot. Wrist action has improved, but it is still stiff and lacks a relaxed backward opening. Reduce upper-arm effort and let the wrist and forearm lead it. Lower your high center of gravity.

You use the wrist actively, but its force is not transferred effectively to the ball and its movement is too large. Reduce wrist range and wait for the ball to fall a little lower, around armpit level, before contact.

Your serving stance is too fixed to use body force. Place the ball in the left palm rather than on the fingers. Keep the racket more vertical and its handle directed toward your body through contact, avoiding an early forward turn that dissipates force. Increase the backswing and weight transfer: after the toss, let the waist and hips carry the arms backward and right, then rotate forward as the ball descends into contact.

The upper arm is positioned well but becomes stiff once raised; relax it. Forearm preparation timing and distance are good, but extend its force-producing movement farther after the backswing. Reduce the oversized wrist action. Contact is too high; wait until the ball falls closer to table height to apply force more comfortably.

Place the ball in the left palm rather than on the fingers. Your preparation posture is too high, with insufficient weight over the left leg. Keep the arms closer to the right side of the chest and rotate farther backward during preparation. Avoid lifting the action backward or turning it prematurely, which finishes force application before contact. Keep the handle directed toward your body rather than behind you.
review_notes: A repeated shoulder/wrist instruction about facing the ground is anatomically unclear and was not expanded.

comment_en: Your upper-arm position and forearm backswing are good, but the upper arm and elbow become rigid. Relax them, continue the forearm farther forward, and reduce wrist movement range. Concentrate forearm and wrist force together. Grip the racket more securely, closing the gap between the handle and hand web.

Your serving posture remains too high; bend the left knee more. Toss from the left palm rather than the fingers. Open the upper arm and forearm during backward preparation, then bring them progressively closer to the body during the forward stroke. Avoid actively pulling the shoulder backward. Keep the handle facing your body, finish toward the left chest, and limit excessive wrist movement rather than directing it behind you.
Your wrist folds too far inward; open it slightly outward. Use a downward forearm and wrist action rather than only moving forward. Contact a little earlier.

Your upper-body posture is too high. Bend forward at the waist and lean into the table. Excessive upper-arm use prevents a complete action. Stabilize the wrist and let the forearm work diagonally from back-right toward front-left, rather than simply pushing straight forward with the wrist and upper arm.

Add a clearer forward press and extension, with effective forward weight movement. Increase the brief force from the forearm and especially the wrist. Move the feet faster and more effectively, keep the wrist open outward rather than folded inward, and relax the upper body.

Lean your weight slightly forward. Reduce excessive upper-arm effort and backward wrist preparation. Keep the wrist stable in an approximately 180-degree alignment with the forearm, and feel the forearm applying the force instead of drawing too far backward.

Your torso is stiff, and the feet only tap without a clear forward press and recovery. Bend at the waist, draw in the abdomen, and reach forward without dropping the shoulder. Relax and open the wrist outward. For the short touch, make the racket more upright, prepare upward, then use a small downward forearm action with only a little wrist force.

Bend the right knee more and lean the upper body into the table. Weight is too far back, leaving the upper arm too far from the body and making you reach for the ball. Contact just after the bounce rather than at the peak or on descent. Stabilize the wrist and feel the forearm controlling contact.
Relax the torso and shoulders, and reduce excessive wrist movement.

Step the right foot farther forward and lean your weight into the table. Reduce upper-arm force and use the forearm instead. After contact, avoid straightening and locking the arm; maintain a controlled bend and a stable wrist.

Contact remains too late, and the racket face tilts back too far, sending the ball high. Make the face more upright, prepare upward, and press downward at contact to keep the return low and short. Use less wrist force. Bend the upright torso forward, draw in the abdomen, open the elbow slightly outward, and add a clear step-in and recovery movement.

Step the right foot farther into the table and lean the upper body forward. Contact just after the bounce. Excessive upper-arm use straightens the arm after contact, possibly because it is held too far from the body and weight is not far enough forward. The wrist also remains straight after contact. Keep the action closer and more controlled.
Bend at the waist, draw in the abdomen, and include waist rotation, which is missing. Load the right foot and reduce the excessive movement ranges of the forearm and wrist.

Adjust toward the right. Your weight is too far back because the waist remains upright. Reduce the large shoulder action and excessive upper-arm force. Let the body lead the shoulder rather than using the shoulder to move the whole body.
Your arm movement is too large; reduce its range.

Your weight moves from the middle to the left instead of from right to left. The grip is too loose, with a large gap beneath the index finger, forcing repeated racket adjustments after each stroke. Secure the grip and finish near the center of the eyebrows rather than beyond the head. Bend the knees more, keep weight over the forefeet, and avoid transferring onto the heels after contact.

Contact remains too far back. Load the right foot during preparation and return weight toward the middle after contact instead of starting in the middle and moving left. Maintain the forward-bent, engaged trunk position throughout. Combine waist rotation and forearm closing at contact. Relax the shoulder and upper arm, keep them supported beside the body, and use a compact forearm action rather than lifting or throwing the arm outward.

Lean forward and bend the knees more, shifting weight slightly right before contact. Shoulder movement is excessive and finishes behind the head. Stop near the center of the eyebrows and let the body lead shoulder force rather than allowing the shoulder to drive the whole action.

Contact earlier. The elbow and upper arm are held too close to the body, making the action cramped. Allow slightly more space and relax the shoulder. Increase the forearm-closing movement and its acceleration at contact.

Weight transfer is reasonably good, but lower your posture and bend the knees more. Do not keep the racket perpendicular to the ground; incline it forward by approximately 10 to 30 degrees during contact.
Draw the arm and racket backward during preparation.
Lower your overall posture and lean farther forward at the waist. Incline the racket forward more. Complete the upper-arm action more fully and continue applying a little forward force after contact.

Core control improves later in the round and compared with the previous video. There is less unnecessary hip movement and more useful waist rotation. Relax the shoulder, contact earlier, and make forearm acceleration more pronounced.
Weight transfer and waist and hip rotation are very good. The racket is too upright at contact; incline it forward instead of keeping it perpendicular to the ground to lower the ball's arc.
Keep the wrist still and relax the body more while bending forward.

The overall action has no major problem. Lower your weight and bend both knees more. Feel the upper arm pressing forward at contact, with the body controlling the block. Avoid an oversized forearm action.

The torso and right shoulder are slightly tense; relax them and let them follow the arm. A somewhat larger forearm action could produce more force after using the incoming ball's momentum, although the coach presents this as optional rather than necessary.
Weight transfer has improved, with better body control of the ball. Lower your center of gravity further by bending the knees more to maintain greater stability.
Relax your shoulders.

review_notes: Only generic encouragement to continue practicing and an ending cue; no substantive technical feedback.

comment_en: Forearm and wrist force application are very good. Add a clear step-in, backward recovery, and renewed step-in sequence instead of keeping the feet fixed. Incline the racket face farther forward and use the wrist to brush forward more rather than only hitting the ball.

The hand controls contact well, but it is disconnected from body movement. Step the right foot farther into the table and lean forward. Shorten the backswing and keep the upper arm closer to the body. Let a small wrist-led movement guide the forearm backward rather than actively pulling the shoulder and elbow back. Coordinate body and hand force.

Wrist movement is excessive and disrupts contact control. Concentrate its force into a brief action with a smaller range. Incline the racket face forward to add brushing. Include a clear step-in, step-back recovery, and renewed step-in sequence.

Do not actively draw the shoulder and elbow far backward during preparation. Control their movement and the upper-arm-to-body angle. Lean the upper body farther into the table and keep the arm closer to the torso during contact.

Smaller wrist movement improves the success rate early in the round, but control declines when you try to apply more force later. Keep wrist force brief and compact, and incline the racket forward to add safer brushing contact. Include step-in and backward recovery footwork. The shoulder and upper arm appear braced; relax during recovery and tighten briefly for the next stroke.

The shoulder action is too large and poorly coordinated with the body. Lean farther into the table and keep the shoulder and upper arm closer to the torso. Avoid actively pulling the shoulder, elbow, and upper arm backward; use only a small wrist and forearm preparation before striking forward. You already have enough force, so focus on a compact, coordinated action.

Leave more space between the upper arm and torso and increase forearm backswing distance to allow preparation time. The racket-face angle is good, but wrist force is missing; add it to the forearm action. Establish stable footing before serving and avoid beginning recovery while still striking.

Your weight-transfer sequence is unclear. The coach describes loading the left leg, shifting briefly right, and returning left with a clear left-foot landing. Adjust the serving grip rather than using the attacking grip: hold mainly with the thumb and index finger, allowing the other fingers to support lightly so that the wrist remains mobile.
review_notes: The timing of the described left-right-left sequence and the exact supporting-finger placement are unclear in the source.

comment_en: Your weight is unstable during contact, and the forearm backswing is too short.

Bend the left knee more before serving and add a clear left-foot landing to transfer weight left afterward. Adjust the grip to improve wrist mobility: hold primarily with the thumb and index finger, allowing the middle, ring, and little fingers to support the racket lightly rather than wrapping tightly around the handle.
The forearm is too close to the body, its backswing is insufficient, and the wrist does not contribute to the serve.

Wrist mobility is insufficient because of the grip. Adjust the middle, ring, and little fingers toward the rear side of the racket, and hold mainly with the thumb and index finger so that the wrist can contribute to the serve.
Bring the right shoulder slightly farther forward.

Brushing and explosive force are good, but the wrist and upper arm contribute too much. Keep the wrist stable and let the forearm drive the upper arm. Apply force more smoothly instead of rushing, allowing a fuller contact action.

Relying only on wrist force can increase errors; add forearm support for a more stable return. Avoid excessive downward or forward right-shoulder movement, and let it relax with the hand. Bring the left shoulder forward with the right rather than leaving it behind. Maintain forward weight, adjust the body with the step-in and recovery, and contact earlier.

Keep weight over the right forefoot and lean the whole body into the table. Acceleration is too abrupt; make force application smoother and allow a fuller contact action to increase brushing and spin.

The early upward wrist action sends the ball high, but it improves later into a forward-downward movement. Maintain that direction and add some forearm force; wrist use itself is good. Include a clear step-in and recovery, and contact earlier. Bring both shoulders forward with the body and hand instead of dropping the right shoulder or leaving the left behind.

Avoid excessive wrist force. Keep the wrist and forearm relatively stable, and apply a brief, controlled forearm force at contact without excessive acceleration. Allow the contact action to continue slightly longer.

Your contact timing and slightly upright racket position are good. Raise the preparation more and press farther downward at contact. Lower your weight and step the right foot farther forward, keeping both feet grounded rather than lifting the left foot for too long. Bring the left shoulder forward together with the right.
You use too much wrist action.

Your contact timing is good, but the left foot begins lifting later in the round; keep it grounded longer. Swing from above downward instead of lifting from below, which sends the return too high. Make the downward press clearer.

Weight control has improved, but the wrist still supplies too much force. Keep the wrist and forearm stable and let the forearm control a downward cut rather than a forward push. The racket is too upright; tilt it back slightly into a flatter position to improve spin.
Prepare the racket upward, then direct the contact action downward.

Your weight control has improved, but the wrist is too loose during contact. Stabilize it with the forearm and let the forearm control the ball. Tilt the racket slightly backward rather than holding it perpendicular to the table to improve brushing.

The right shoulder remains stiff; relax it. The forearm-closing path is good, but increase its brief force and acceleration. Waist force still does not reach the racket effectively, so strengthen the coordinated burst from waist rotation.
Your backward preparation is generally good, but turn backward rather than downward. Forward force is insufficient. Increase waist and hip rotation toward the front-left during the stroke.

Open the elbow slightly backward and outward, leaving roughly two or three fist-widths between it and the waist. Keep it controlled rather than pulling it inward during contact. Relax the upper arm and lower the left shoulder so that both shoulders are more level. Coordinate waist rotation and forearm closing so their force acts together.
The overall action has no major problem. Avoid folding the shoulder and elbow too far inward; open them slightly backward. Transfer weight a little farther from right to left during contact.

Waist, shoulder, and hand movement are too separated. Relax the shoulder and let a quicker waist turn bring the hand through in a more connected action. Avoid folding the wrist inward; open it outward and keep it stable while closing the forearm. The left shoulder rises while the right sinks; keep both shoulders more level.

Lower your weight and bend the knees more. After contact, transfer farther onto the left leg instead of remaining on the right. Open the shoulder and arm slightly outward and backward and maintain that position rather than actively thrusting forward. Raising the upper arm slightly may help.
Avoid folding the wrist inward. Lower the left shoulder slightly and open the posture enough to relax the movement. Your forward waist bend and abdominal engagement are good; maintain them.

Weight transfer has improved. Keep the core controlled after contact and shift weight slightly left through hip rotation rather than swinging the hips indiscriminately. Shoulder and arm movement is better, but the upper arm should continue farther forward after contact.

Contact timing varies between the peak and descent; consistently meet the ball around its highest point. Use less of your own force for the block and redirect the incoming ball with a relaxed action. Waist and arm force become better coordinated later in the round, which is a substantial improvement. Open the inward-folded wrist slightly outward and relax the right shoulder.
Control the forearm's force and feel the upper arm pressing forward while using the incoming ball's momentum.

review_notes: Only promotional requests to like, subscribe, share, and donate; no coaching feedback.

comment_en: Your defensive action is too large. Keep the forearm stable rather than actively applying excessive force. Use the body to control contact and maintain stable body and shoulder positioning.

Your rhythm is disrupted by repeated attempts to apply force and slow recovery. Relax and use a small arm-and-waist movement to absorb and redirect the incoming ball. Lower and relax the right shoulder. Coordinate waist rotation and forearm closing instead of letting the waist fling the hand around. Forearm explosiveness is good but excessive for this block; use less and open the wrist slightly outward.
Keep the body centered, lower your weight, and bend the knees more. Support the block with stable body control rather than excessive force, maintaining a steady defensive action.

You step in too late, sometimes only after contact. Advance the step and reduce the oversized forearm path. Wrist explosiveness is good; combine it with a forward-inclined racket face to brush the ball and add spin. Move both shoulders and the body forward together instead of reaching with the right arm while leaving the torso behind. Keep the hand and ball closer to the body.

Weight transfer and stepping are good, but lean forward at the waist as you step. Keep the upper arm closer to the body during preparation. Let the wrist and forearm lead the upper arm rather than the reverse. Make the oversized movement more compact to concentrate force.

Impact force has increased, and wrist force is good, but the flick needs more brushing rather than impact alone. Adjust the racket toward a flatter, forward-inclined face and shorten the forearm path to produce a more spinning return. Move the left shoulder and whole body forward with the right hand, and step in earlier.

The action is too large, dispersing force. Keep the arm bent before contact rather than straightening it. Reduce the angles between forearm and upper arm and between upper arm and body, bringing the action closer so that body and shoulder force combine effectively.
Wrist force is not being transferred effectively to the ball.

Waist rotation and coordination with the ball are good. Toss from the center of the left palm, not the fingers. Bend the left knee more and step the left leg forward into the described crossed stance to improve weight transfer. The wrist is stiff because of the grip. Hold mainly with the thumb and index finger, letting the remaining fingers rest lightly against the left side of the handle rather than gripping tightly.
Relax the forearm during the backswing.

review_notes: Repeated tossing-hand instruction says to place the wrist in the palm; both language versions are unintelligible, so no correction was invented.

comment_en: Avoid retracting the upper arm backward during preparation, and relax the forearm and wrist.
review_notes: An unrelated or corrupted breathing instruction was omitted.

comment_en: Weight transfer and force coordination have improved. Place the ball in the left palm rather than on the fingers. The serve still relies too much on the arms and too little on wrist force. Adjust the grip so that the thumb and index finger hold the racket while the other three fingers rest lightly against the handle's side, allowing a freer figure-eight wrist action.

Wrist force is good, but the racket face is too upright; flatten it to brush the lower part of the ball. Step in and contact earlier to improve the disrupted rhythm. Shorten the forearm swing and favor wrist contribution. Bring the left shoulder forward with the right and the body. Relax the upright torso, bend at the waist, and draw in the abdomen as you move with the hand.

The left hand stays behind and the body shifts left. Bring the left hand beside the body, soften the chest, and draw in the abdomen instead of keeping the waist rigidly upright. Use the forearm to brush the ball, applying force promptly without stiffness and allowing a fuller contact action.

Advance both the step-in and contact timing and shorten the forearm backswing. Wrist use is very good; earlier contact should make it more reliable. Bring the left shoulder forward with the right rather than leaving it behind. Your forward waist bend and abdominal engagement are present, but the trailing left shoulder makes the posture look stiff.

The backswing is too large and leaves too little time for contact. Shorten it and extend the forward contact action, while brushing the bottom of the ball rather than pushing into its side. Apply force promptly but avoid excessive acceleration.

Your success rate has improved. Shorten the forearm backswing and coordinate it with a clearer, brief burst of wrist force. Your left shoulder still stays behind; bring it forward together with your right shoulder.

Your push is too stiff. Relax and make softer contact, using a smaller backswing and a longer forward motion through the ball instead of abruptly accelerating at contact. Your waist is too upright; soften your chest and draw in your abdomen.
review_notes: The source also calls for quick force application, which is not clearly reconciled with its instruction against acceleration at contact.

comment_en: If the intended stroke is a short touch, use a more upright racket face, prepare upward and press downward to keep the return short. Step in and contact the ball earlier, reduce the forearm and wrist motion, and open the wrist outward rather than inward. Bend at the waist, engage the abdomen and bring the torso forward with the step, keeping the forward pressure controlled. Bring your left shoulder forward with your right.
review_notes: The coach explicitly expresses uncertainty about whether the stroke is a short touch.

comment_en: Lean farther into the table, soften your chest and avoid keeping the waist so upright. You use too much force in the first half, although this improves later. Contact the ball just after the bounce; your current late contact makes the placement harder to control. Develop a better feel for applying forearm force through contact.
Bring your shoulders forward with the stroke instead of leaving them behind; the comments identify this problem in both the right and left shoulder.

Your left hand stays behind and causes your body to lean left. Keep it beside the torso and let it follow the upper body so that you face forward. Shorten the backswing and overall movement. Your contact point has improved, but it still needs to become consistent.

The quicker action is better. Keep the racket face more upright and prepare upward instead of backward. Your wrist action is fine; add more downward forearm action to lower the ball's arc. As you step in with the right foot, bring the left shoulder forward with your body.

Your contact is late, possibly because the preparation is too large and makes you miss the early part of the bounce. Shorten the backswing and overall range so that you can control an earlier contact point.
Contact the ball earlier and coordinate the waist and hand so that they apply force together instead of separately.

Your overall movement and waist and hip rotation are good. Raise the forearm for the backward preparation instead of letting it hang down. Increase the backward preparation through the waist and hips, moving the right foot half a step back to make room for this rotation.

You contact the ball earlier than before, which is an improvement, but the timing should still move forward. Your waist applies force after your hand; combine the waist rotation and forearm closing at impact. Relax the shoulder and reduce its oversized movement, relying more on coordinated waist and forearm action.

Your stroke is very complete. Raise the forearm during preparation and turn backward instead of letting it drop. Move the right foot half a step back to allow a larger backward turn of the waist and hips.

Your waist and hand act separately, with the waist, shoulder and hand moving in sequence and the hand being flung through. Use a quicker, brief waist action together with the forearm at contact. Reduce the effort from the hand and use core tightening and rotation. Contact the ball earlier, rather than beside your body, and incline the racket face forward for more brushing.
Your overall movement is very good, but the weight transfer needs improvement. Finish by shifting toward the left leg so that the whole body contributes power to the ball.
review_notes: The source places the weight on the left leg both before and after contact while requesting a transfer. The intended starting leg is unresolved.

comment_en: Increase your backswing. Your forearm closing action is excellent.

Your body is stiff and the stroke is incomplete; extend the forearm farther forward. Bend your knees to lower your center of gravity. Recover after each shot so that you have enough time for the next one and can maintain a smoother rhythm.

Your rhythm is uneven, making it difficult to judge the ball's position and height. Lower your center of gravity and start preparing earlier so that the backswing is not rushed or too short. As a tall player, finish in front of your chest rather than your nose, with more forward pressure.

Your posture and stroke completeness have improved somewhat, but more adjustment is needed. Bend your knees further and prepare by turning the waist and hips to the right before contact, rather than only turning left afterward. Let the upper arm travel farther forward to complete the stroke toward the left eyebrow.

Your backswing is too short; use more waist rotation to take the racket back. Close the forearm forward with a pressing action instead of finishing toward your nose. Incline the racket face forward to control the balls that are going long.

Bend your knees to lower your high center of gravity. Increase the backward preparation through the hips, which currently rotate too little. Let the upper arm move farther forward and use the hips to help complete the stroke.

Relax your stiff shoulder and upper arm and turn the waist farther to the right during preparation. Use the incoming ball's force rather than staying tense, and wait for the ball to rise a little before contact.
Bend your knees to lower your center of gravity and relax your wrist. Let the waist lead the whole body's movement instead of playing the stroke with the hand alone.

The brief force from your forearm closing is good. Increase the small backswing and turn the waist farther right to generate more power. Wait for the ball to reach its peak instead of rushing into a stiff contact.
Your upper-body posture and hand action have improved, but you still need more knee bend. Lower your body and coordinate its force with the stroke instead of relying on the hand alone.

Your right foot is too far forward; place it slightly behind the left to allow the waist to turn right. Increase the waist turn and backward preparation so that the stroke is not driven by the hand alone. Wait a little longer for the ball to rise before contact.

Bend your knees and feel your weight on the forefeet to lower your center of gravity. Transfer weight from right to left instead of keeping both feet planted without a shift. Increase the waist rotation and backward hip preparation, letting the hips carry the shoulder back to cushion the movement before the hit.

Lower your center of gravity and press the arm forward. Incline the racket face forward and brush the ball more instead of mainly hitting it. Give yourself a longer preparation to load the stroke, relax the shoulder and use more wrist brushing rather than lifting with the upper arm.
review_notes: An additional instruction about the upper body's presence is too vague to interpret precisely.

comment_en: Step the right foot into the table, with the right foot ahead of the left, and load the right forefoot. You use too much forearm force and keep the wrist stiff; relax both so that the flick is less forced.

Your posture is too upright. Bring the shoulders and weight forward and allow more preparation. Use wrist preparation and brushing instead of relying only on the thigh and shoulder. Your timing is good, but stop the wrist action sooner after contact because the follow-through is too long.

Your weight positioning and wrist force have improved. Step the right foot farther in and lean the whole body forward. The forearm still dominates despite the better wrist action; relax the wrist, prepare it backward and use its force instead of relying on the forearm alone.

Your early strokes are excellent and the timing is good, but later the racket angle becomes inconsistent. Keep the face inclined forward and flick with forward wrist pressure instead of lifting the upper arm. Increase the backward preparation to load the stroke.
Your wrist action and contact have improved. The main remaining issue is the footwork: step the right foot into the table, shift the weight forward onto it and lean the upper body in.

Your upper body is too loose and rotates too far left while the feet remain still. Make a larger preparation backward and to the right, then finish facing forward rather than continuing left. Keep the grip relaxed during preparation and tighten it clearly at contact instead of simply moving smoothly through the ball.

Your upper-body and waist rotation are good, but the weight distribution is wrong. Start with the left foot forward and the right foot behind, then add a clear landing on the left foot so that the weight finishes there instead of on the right. Stand closer to the table and place the ball securely in the left palm for the toss.
review_notes: The source's contrast between two palm positions is unintelligible; only the clear instruction to use the palm is retained.

comment_en: You rotate too far left. Increase the backward and rightward preparation, then stop facing forward. Your relaxed preparation is good, but tighten the grip at contact and use a brief wrist action. The current smooth push lacks a clear transition from relaxation to force and produces a lower-quality serve.

Your upper-body action is good, but your weight does not finish on the left foot. Add a clear left-foot landing and press the body left rather than leaning backward to the right. The large serving motion and low toss make you miss the best contact point and send the ball too high; toss higher, as your higher tosses already produce better serves and arcs. Hold the ball securely in the left palm.
review_notes: The source's contrast between palm and hand placement is unclear.

comment_en: Your backward and rightward preparation is too small, while the follow-through to the left is too long. Take the forearm farther back to the right, then stop in front without extra leftward waist rotation. Add a brief wrist action with a clear transition from a relaxed to a firm grip, and flatten the racket face to lower the ball's arc.

Toss the ball from the left palm rather than the fingers. Your timing is inconsistent and the first bounce is sometimes too close to your body, producing a high arc; aim for the first bounce near the middle of your own half. The weight transfer has not improved, so add a clear left-foot landing and press the weight left.

You step in and then stay fixed, without recovering and stepping again to find the next ball. Use more footwork to adjust your position. Flatten the racket face, brush the underside with stronger wrist action and contact the rising ball earlier. Relax the shoulder and keep the upper-arm backswing small.

Your shoulder backswing is too large. Keep the action in front and to the right, directing force forward. Tilt the overly upright racket face back slightly and make the stroke smaller and more stable, with the body leading the force.

Your footwork has improved and you are finding the ball better. The wrist's brief force is still weak; flatten the racket face and brush underneath with more wrist action. Contact the ball earlier, just as it rises, and shorten the backswing by reducing the forearm movement.

Your backswing is too large and the wrist is loose. Stabilize the wrist and forearm, letting the forearm lead the upper arm rather than adding independent upper-arm force. Use a smaller preparation and direct the motion forward through contact.

Your foot positioning is good, but contact is too far back. Meet the ball earlier and use more wrist force; the coach advises against slicing downward in this clip. Lean your weight farther forward and bring the left shoulder forward with the right instead of leaving it behind.

Your contact feel and wrist adjustment have improved, but they remain inconsistent. Keep the wrist and forearm stable, reduce the forearm's backward preparation and move directly forward. Flatten the racket face and shorten the stroke.

Your step-in timing is good. Firm the grip briefly at contact to absorb the incoming force and keep the ball short, rather than only pressing downward with the hand. Bring the left shoulder forward with the right, prepare upward and cut downward.

Your overall movement is good and the timing is very good. Tilt the overly vertical racket face back to add brushing. Shift more weight onto the right side as you step into the table and use the body to control the stroke.
You use the wrist more effectively in the latter half, absorbing the incoming force to keep the return short. Your timing is good. Prepare upward and press downward through the ball.

The racket face is too vertical, so the ball goes into the net and lacks brushing and spin. Tilt the face back and control the stroke with the forearm instead of pushing with the upper arm. Move your weight forward from its rearward position and keep the upper arm closer to the body.

Your timing is good. Add more sideways and backward preparation before pressing down to absorb the incoming force. Move from a relaxed grip to a briefly firm grip at contact as the wrist applies downward force.

Your racket face is too vertical, sending the ball into the net without enough brushing. Tilt it back and give the forearm more forward movement through contact instead of merely touching the ball. The racket angle is the main problem.

You rely too much on the forearm and lift it excessively. Use more waist rotation and shift your weight forward to press the ball down. Increase the backward and rightward preparation, incline the racket face forward and brush the ball more.

Your center of gravity is too high. Keep the forearm raised as you prepare backward instead of dropping it. Let the waist and hips actively rotate the upper body, rather than having the shoulders pull the waist around, and keep your weight on the forefeet.

You grip the racket too tightly, restricting its adjustment. Relax the hand and wrist, turn the waist more during preparation and combine waist force with the forearm instead of relying on the arm alone. Lean your weight forward, incline the racket face forward and brush the ball. Avoid lifting with the upper arm.

Your center of gravity stays too high, leaving the upper and lower body disconnected and preventing the legs, hips and waist from contributing at contact. Sink lower and feel both feet driving against the ground so that the whole body's force reaches the ball.

In the first half, the arm supplies enough force to help the ball land, but later the upper arm stiffens and the grip tightens, reducing consistency. Turn the waist farther right and increase the backswing to load the stroke. At contact, combine waist rotation with forearm closing and lean forward. Add brushing instead of relying on a hard hit to keep the ball stable.

review_notes: All source rows contain only the word 'big'; no interpretable technical feedback is available.

comment_en: Continue closing the forearm through the stroke.

Your waist and hip rotation are fairly good, but your center of gravity is too high, especially because the knees do not bend enough. The stroke is too small and the upper arm stays close against the body, preventing the upper arm and shoulder from contributing force. Increase the angle between the upper arm and torso and direct the stroke forward.

Your shoulder, upper arm, forearm and wrist remain stiff. Increase the distance between the wrist and waist, and rotate the arm and waist together. Apply their force together as the forearm closes instead of using the waist to fling the arm through.

Your upper-arm action and coordination show improvement, but the upper arm remains too close to the body, making the shoulder and arm stiff and leaving the forearm and wrist to supply the force. Increase the angle between the right upper arm and torso and relax before contact. Bend your knees more to lower your high center of gravity.
review_notes: The opening praise is fragmented in the source; its precise description of coordination is unclear.

comment_en: Your upper arm, forearm and wrist are held too tightly together; open the action out and relax. Apply waist rotation and forearm force together instead of using the waist to pull the forearm through.

Bend the knees farther and lean the waist forward. Increase the angle between the upper arm and torso, then maintain it within a stable range rather than applying force with the arm pressed against the body.
Your arm is held too close to the body. Move the wrist farther away, shorten the action and use only a little wrist force.

Your overall movement is sound, and you control the racket well through the waist and body. Bend lower and increase the angle between the upper arm and torso, keeping it within a stable range. The main problem is upper-arm stiffness, which opening this angle should help.
Your wrist is still too close to the body, and even the left hand looks tense. Move the wrist farther out and lean your weight forward. Keep the action compact and contact the ball a little later.
Your center of gravity is too high because the knees do not bend enough. Increase the small angle between the upper arm and torso and keep it stable instead of holding the arm against the body.

The forearm backswing goes too far back. Stop with the racket slightly in front of your side rather than beside the body, and keep the preparation small. Use the waist to guide the forearm, borrow the incoming ball's force and return it instead of generating all the force yourself.
review_notes: A final fragment appears to request self-generated force, contrary to the preceding complete instruction.

comment_en: Your center of gravity is too high, with insufficient knee bend and an overly straight waist. Bend the knees and lean farther forward. Increase the angle between the upper arm and torso; the coach suggests moving the forearm outward to the right or lifting the shoulder to open this angle.

Keep the right wrist from moving too far away from the body. Your upper arm and forearm are extremely stiff; relax them, shorten the action and use more wrist power. Lean your weight forward and bring the left shoulder forward instead of leaving it behind.

The feel of your flick's force is fairly good. Step the right foot forward into the table, lean forward and feel the right toes gripping the ground. Avoid letting the body drift left after the stroke.
review_notes: Most instructions place the weight on the right leg, but one source sentence says to control it on the left leg. The intended finishing support is contradictory.

comment_en: You rely too much on the shoulder to hit and adjust the ball. Relax it and use the forearm and especially the wrist. For a ball in front, step forward with the right foot instead of only pressing the body forward.

Step the right foot farther forward, keeping it ahead of the left, and lean your weight onto it instead of drifting left. Bend forward at the waist, soften the chest and draw in the abdomen. Relax the wrist and grip before contact, then tighten the grip at impact to feel the transition from relaxation to force.

Your wrist produces good force, but the stroke is too much of a direct hit. Brush the side of the ball more and reduce the straight backward-to-forward impact. Step in with the right foot instead of only reaching with the body. Relax the shoulder and use the wrist and forearm to power the stroke.

Your center of gravity is too high and too far left. Step the right leg forward, grip the ground with the right foot and lean forward. The racket finishes too upright; use the fingers to turn it forward at contact and finish with the face at roughly 45 degrees rather than perpendicular to the table.
Relax the shoulder and use the waist and abdominal muscles together as a coordinated whole.

Adjust the serving grip from your attacking grip: move the middle, ring and little fingers slightly back against one side of the handle instead of wrapping them tightly around it. This allows the thumb and index finger to contribute more and frees the wrist. Increase the backward movement of the upper arm and forearm and the waist turn, then combine forward waist and hip rotation with a left-foot landing to strengthen the serve and spin.

You begin to use the waist and abdomen later in the clip, but mainly on the left side. Engage the whole waist and abdomen. Take the forearm farther back without lifting the shoulder and upper arm, and flatten the racket face to brush the underside of the ball for more spin.

Your center of gravity is a little high. Bend the knees more, especially the left knee. Increase the backward preparation through the upper arm, waist and hips. As the left hand tosses the ball, let the waist carry the upper arm and forearm backward to the right, then turn forward and left as the ball falls.

Your preparation does not fully load the serve. Relax the hand, elbow and shoulder, take the upper arm and forearm farther back and show a clearer transition from relaxation to tightening. Flatten the racket face to brush the lower side of the ball for more spin. Use the whole waist and abdomen instead of only dropping the left side.
review_notes: A source row is an editorial instruction to combine sentences, rather than coaching feedback; it was excluded.

comment_en: Adding the left-foot stamp helps your waist turn left and contributes force. However, the backward and rightward rotation remains too small. Increase that preparation so that the stroke has more than just leftward force and can produce greater speed and power at contact.

Your step-in timing is very good. Cut a little more downward with the wrist instead of making such a flat stroke, which will lower the ball's arc. Bring the left shoulder slightly forward and lean your weight forward as well.

Step the right foot about half a step farther forward and right. The main issue is the high upper-body position: lean farther forward at the waist and shorten the distance between the body and racket so that the body controls the ball better.

Your brief wrist force is good, but the wrist moves too much and makes the ball unstable. Use a smaller, more concentrated burst. Give the upper arm more space from the torso during preparation instead of pinning it close, and contact the ball a little earlier.
Avoid using too much wrist force. Stabilize the wrist relative to the forearm and let the forearm drive the stroke. Lean the upper-body weight a little farther forward.

Reduce the excessive wrist force and shorten its action. Brush downward across the lower half of the ball instead of lifting forward and upward. Give the upper arm more space from the body, reach the hand forward and contact the ball earlier without dropping the right shoulder. Relax the overly tight grip.

Your overall movement is very good, but the wrist is too loose. Stabilize it relative to the forearm and use the forearm to control the stroke. This should reduce errors and improve control of the ball's arc and spin.

Your step-in timing becomes more consistent in the latter half. Stop pressing the shoulder downward to reach the ball; give the upper arm more space from the body, relax and let the racket find the contact point. Your wrist action is good, but the racket face is too flat and sends the ball high. Make it slightly more upright to absorb the force better.

Contact the ball just after the bounce instead of at its highest point, where placement and a two-bounce short return become harder to control. Stabilize the wrist and forearm and use the forearm to brush the ball rather than pushing with the upper arm. Lean the upper body farther forward and feel the body leading the shoulder into the stroke.

Your upper arm and shoulder are too stiff. Relax them, allow more space between the upper arm and torso and let the racket find the ball. Use a slightly more upright face to cut and absorb the force, keeping the return shorter and lower. Contact the ball earlier, because the late timing is disrupting your rhythm.

The main issue is the contact point. Meet the ball just after the bounce rather than at its peak, where the arc and placement are harder to control. Lean your weight farther into the table to reach the best contact point.

Your contact is too late and the return's arc is too high. Make the racket face slightly more upright and cut downward to lower the ball. Open the upper arm away from the torso a little and relax both the arm and shoulder, letting the racket find the ball without reaching excessively far from the body.

Your contact remains too late. Meeting the ball at its peak prevents an effective brush for a short return. Lean farther into the table and contact it just after the bounce to find the best timing for keeping it short.

You seem rushed and too eager to get the ball onto the table. Relax, turn the waist farther backward and right and enlarge the swing instead of relying on a small hand-driven action. Open the upper arm away from the body rather than holding it tightly against the torso.

Your explosive force is fairly good, but your center of gravity is too high and the weight transfer is unclear. Load farther onto the right before contact instead of starting in the middle and only pushing left. Enlarge the action, increase the angle between the upper arm and torso and move the forearm outward so that the upper arm can contribute rather than leaving the work to the forearm.

You still hit mainly with the hand without enough backward and rightward waist preparation. Increase the waist turn and backswing, incline the racket face forward and brush the side of the ball for greater stability. Keep roughly two fists of space between the elbow and torso and relax the elbow and shoulder. Combine waist and arm force instead of flinging the arm into the ball.

Your center of gravity is too high, especially in the lower body, because your knees do not bend enough. You use the forearm without enough upper-arm contribution. Increase the angle between the upper arm and torso and move the forearm outward.

You hit the ball too directly and rely on the arm without enough backward preparation and waist rotation. Turn farther backward and right and use more waist force. Keep about two fists of space between the elbow and torso, open the upper arm away from the body and relax the shoulder. This will give the preparation and forearm closing more room; add brushing instead of mainly impacting the ball.

Bend your knees more to lower your high center of gravity. Increase the angle between the upper arm and torso and let the upper arm apply more forward force instead of relying only on the forearm. Complete the stroke toward the left eyebrow.
Relax the shoulders, keep them level and avoid lifting them together. Use more forearm force as you close the stroke and increase the waist rotation. Make the release of force clearer and stronger.

Your waist and hip rotation are good, but the lower-body weight is unstable. Finish with more weight on the left rather than the right. The left leg lifts slightly after contact, showing that the weight is staying on the right.

Both shoulders remain stiff, and the left hand blocks the front of the chest and interferes with the action. Your right forearm action is very good. Add more waist rotation and a longer backswing before closing the forearm to generate more force.

Your overall technique is fairly standard, but the weight position and transfer need work. Bend the knees more, lean the upper body forward and sink lower. Feel the feet gripping the ground and keep the weight on the forefeet rather than the heels.

Both shoulders are too tense, preventing the existing waist rotation from transmitting force to the hand and racket. Relax the shoulders so that the waist and arm force can reach the racket. Start preparing earlier, allow more backswing and stop the racket after completing the hit.
Lower your high center of gravity. Keep the weight on the right before contact and shift it slightly left afterward.

You stand too far back, contact the ball too late and make the stroke too large. Stand closer and use a smaller action in front of the body to borrow the incoming force. Relax both shoulders and lower the left hand from the front of the chest.
Your center of gravity is too high; lean the upper body farther forward. Avoid bending the wrist excessively and adjust the wrist and fingers downward.

You still stand too far back, make an oversized stroke and contact the ball too late. Lean your body and weight forward and shorten the action. Your waist rotation is good, but the wrist is stiff and lacks a clear sense of applying force. Relax and use the incoming ball's force.

Your center of gravity remains high. Lean the upper body forward and allow the right shoulder to lower slightly. Stabilize the loose wrist before contact, aligning it with the forearm at about 180 degrees instead of bending it too far backward.
Stand closer to the table and relax both shoulders, especially the left.
Bend the knees more to lower your high center of gravity and keep the weight forward. Stabilize the wrist instead of letting it remain too loose.

You rely too much on the forearm, making the stroke resemble a topspin swing. Shorten the action and use more wrist brushing to flick the ball up. Make a clear forward step instead of remaining stationary, and relax both shoulders.

Your overall movement is fairly good. Move the weight forward from the heels and feel the forefeet and toes gripping the ground. Relax the stiff wrist and use the fingers to rotate the racket forward through contact. Finish with the racket face angled to the table rather than vertical, using finger rotation instead of simply pushing the wrist forward.

Relax the right shoulder and release the stiffness in the left shoulder and upper arm, which are held too close to the torso. Use less forearm and more wrist brushing. Improve the step-in and recovery between balls instead of staying in place, and move the contact point slightly forward.
Direct the finger force farther forward with a pressing action.

Add a clear step-in and recovery. Your forearm range is acceptable, but use more wrist force to adjust the ball and move the contact point forward. Relax the stiff left shoulder and hand, keeping the hand beside the body.

You use only the upper arm and forearm, without bringing the wrist and fingers into the stroke. Relax the wrist at contact instead of keeping it stiff and feel the index finger rotating forward to apply force.

Your toss is not high enough and your weight starts shifting before the serve is complete. Establish a stable stance first. Increase the forearm backswing to create a clearer loading phase; the current short preparation produces weak serves.
Lean the upper body forward and stand with the left foot ahead of the right. Turn the body, shoulder and arm backward, then time the forward rotation so that the ball meets the racket face.
The right upper arm and elbow are too close to the body. Open them out to create more space and relax the right shoulder.

You serve mainly with the shoulder, without transferring force from the feet into the upper body. Bend the knees and make a larger backward turn through the upper arm and hips as you toss. Rotate forward as the ball falls so that the body's force reaches the ball.
Move the wrist farther from the body and establish a stable stance before serving.

You toss before completing the preparation and settling your stance, so the feet and weight cannot contribute to the serve. Plant both feet first, with the left ahead of the right, then toss. As you toss, let the upper arm lead the waist and hips backward, then rotate naturally forward as the ball falls to apply the body's force.
Lower the left hand from its high position to the side of the waist. Apply a stronger, more explosive burst of force with the right wrist.
Step the right foot into the table. Shorten the backward preparation and increase the forward movement through and after contact.
Use more wrist force to improve the quality of the return.
Feel the forearm controlling the ball rather than the wrist, keeping the connection between them stable. Reduce the oversized backswing and increase the forward motion through contact.
Make the step-in more distinct, then recover and step in again for the next ball instead of remaining fixed. Make the wrist's explosive force clearer as well.
Your wrist is loose; keep it stable. Reduce the backward preparation to a compact range and extend the forward action to lengthen the contact and improve the return.

Relax both shoulders, especially the right, and let the right shoulder settle instead of lifting it. Make the racket face more upright and add a clearer downward cut as you press forward, with a more distinct wrist burst. Step forward, recover backward and step in again.

Your weight control is fairly good, but the preparation is too large. Contact the ball just after it bounces on your side rather than at or after its peak. Reduce the backswing and give more of the movement to the forward stroke.
Your shoulders become increasingly raised later in the clip; relax them. Make the overly flat racket face more upright and make the footwork more distinct.

Your contact is too late. Meet the ball just after the bounce, when you can combine with its force most effectively. Stabilize the loose wrist, feel the forearm applying force and avoid taking the racket too far back.
Make the wrist force more distinct and increase the racket face's angle to the table. Use clearer footwork, stepping in, recovering and stepping in again for each ball.
Your overall movement has improved. Keep the contact point just after the ball bounces.
Your forearm closing is good, but the waist's force is not being combined with it.
Your weight is too far back on the heels. Lean forward at the waist and use the fingers to rotate the racket counterclockwise, pressing the index finger against the racket face to apply force.
Relax the right shoulder and keep the left hand in front of the chest. Your contact is a little late; meet the ball earlier.

Lean the whole body forward, especially at the waist, and soften the chest. Your grip is too loose at contact; lower the index finger slightly and feel it rotating forward to apply force. Avoid bending the wrist too far backward during preparation. Adjust it forward so that it aligns with the forearm at 180 degrees at contact, without extending beyond that.
Relax the right shoulder, avoid bending the wrist backward and contact the ball earlier.

Soften the chest by bringing both shoulders slightly forward. Lower the index finger from its high position so that its force acts more effectively on the racket. Bend the knees further to lower and stabilize the body's weight.

Your footwork rhythm is good, but you drop the shoulder instead of using enough backward waist rotation and explosive waist force. Let the waist carry the arm farther back during preparation. Contact the ball near its highest point rather than waiting for it to descend.

Your center of gravity is too high. Bend the knees more and lean forward at the waist. Adjust the wrist slightly outward and backward rather than folding it inward, aiming for roughly 180-degree alignment with the forearm at contact.
Your wrist is a little stiff.
review_notes: The source also mentions lowering the shoulder blade, but does not specify whether this is an observation or a correction.

comment_en: Increase the backward waist rotation and relax before contact instead of remaining stiff throughout. The wrist folds too far inward; open it outward slightly.
Your forearm and wrist are stiff, and your contact point is too far back.

Shift the weight onto the forefeet and bend the knees more. Adjust the wrist outward and the back of the hand backward until the wrist and forearm form a straight, 180-degree line, without bending to either side of that alignment. Relax the wrist before applying force instead of keeping it tense throughout.

Your force application is good, but in defense you should borrow more of the opponent's force instead of generating it all yourself. Relax and redirect the incoming ball. Your contact is too late and beside the body; meet the ball in front at roughly a 45-degree position.

Your action is too large, especially through the forearm. Keep it closer to the body instead of taking a downward backswing to generate force. In defense, use the incoming force with upper-arm and shoulder rotation rather than actively powering the stroke through a forearm backswing. Bend the knees, lean forward and keep the whole posture lower and more compact.
Your rhythm is good. Avoid flinging the forearm and do not drop the shoulder.

Your movement is too large and your center of gravity is too high. Raise the forearm slightly instead of letting the wrist drop, and feel the upper arm and shoulder pushing forward through contact. Avoid actively generating the stroke's force with the forearm.
Your core is unsteady and you use too much shoulder force, with substantial forearm effort as well. Meet the ball diagonally in front of the body.
review_notes: The source's negative description of the current contact point is corrupted; its requested forward position is clear.

comment_en: You stand too upright. Lean forward at the waist and bend both knees more. Keep the forearm, upper arm and shoulder coordinated within one stable action, without an extra independent burst from one part. In particular, reduce the large forearm movement and force, borrowing the opponent's force instead.

Your wrist's explosive action is good, but it remains somewhat stiff. Relax the wrist and shoulder, allow more preparation before stepping in and incline the racket face forward to brush the ball. Your body is rising upright; keep your weight leaning forward.

Your step-in position and right-leg placement are good, but the upper body stays too high. Contact the ball in front rather than at your side. The arm pulls too far sideways and the angle between the upper arm and torso is too large; direct the upper arm forward instead.
Your contact is too late. Add more brushing to the stroke.
review_notes: The source's explanation of reduced friction and its instruction about moving the impact backward are unclear and potentially inconsistent with the timing correction.

comment_en: Your overall force application is fairly good. Lean the upper body farther into the table, reduce the angle between the upper arm and torso and shorten the distance between the body and racket.
Your wrist force has increased, but flatten the racket face and add more brushing. When stepping in, bring the body forward with the foot instead of leaving it behind. Use less forearm force.

The shoulder seems disconnected from the body. Start slightly closer to the middle and step diagonally forward and right instead of stepping straight forward and reaching right with the shoulder. Keep the contact point around the one-o'clock direction and shorten the distance between the upper arm and torso.

Your wrist force is very good, but you lift and fling the shoulder and upper arm too high. Avoid throwing the upper arm too far back on its own; turn the waist with it. The knees are stiff and the waist contributes little, leaving only hand force. Bring the waist into the serve and flatten the racket face.
Your body does not rotate through and your weight does not transfer. Open the tossing hand flat and place the ball in the center of the palm.
The forearm and wrist preparation are good, but the upper arm is held too high and the serve lacks a brief explosive release. Stay relaxed during the backswing.

Lean the body farther forward. Start with the weight on the left leg, shift it slightly backward after the toss and let waist and hip rotation carry the shoulder back. As you move forward, return the weight to the left leg and rotate the waist, hips and shoulder together so that the whole body's force reaches the ball.
Make a clear transition from a relaxed hand during preparation to a firm grip as you apply force.

Your elbow action and explosive force are very good. The main issue is the missing side-to-side weight transfer. Add a left-foot landing and turn the waist sufficiently backward as you toss so that the body can contribute more force to the ball.

Your racket is too upright. Flatten it slightly to brush the lower side of the ball. Step in earlier so that the stroke is less rushed. Relax the lowered, pressing shoulder and extend the right forearm forward easily.

Your overall action is very good, especially the contact point and control of force. Lean the upper-body weight farther forward and shorten the distance to the racket for better body control. Lower the wrist slightly from its raised position, keep it stable and feel the forearm applying force at contact.

Your step-in timing remains late. Step in earlier, recover and step in again for the next ball. Do not deliberately press the shoulder downward to apply force; simply bring it forward and extend the upper arm and forearm slightly.

Your overall movement is sound. Avoid moving the wrist backward before contact; keep it stable, hold the racket firmly with the fingers and direct more force forward without changing the racket angle. Soften the chest and bend forward rather than keeping the waist straight, bringing the body into a more compact position to control the ball.
Press the arm and right shoulder forward.
Your force application, timing and ball quality are very good. Direct the index finger's force forward instead of relying on the wrist. Lower the hand slightly to find that finger-driven feeling.
Use more wrist action and step in earlier; the current step-in timing is late.

Your waist is too upright. The first two contact points are inaccurate, although they improve later. Meet the ball just after the bounce, stabilize the loose wrist relative to the forearm and use the forearm and fingers to apply force.

The wrist begins to wobble, and your body does not lean forward even when you step in. Keep the wrist action small and direct the racket from high to low. Lean forward with the step, relax the shoulder and avoid pressing it down. Let the shoulder serve as a connection while the forearm and wrist do the main work.

Your center of gravity is too high at contact. Bring the shoulders slightly inward and lean forward. Hold the handle securely with the fingers, keep the racket and wrist stable and lower the raised wrist. Coordinate the index finger's force with the action.
The strokes at the beginning of this clip are good. Maintain that same action throughout.

Your upper body is too upright, leaving the racket too far away and making the contact timing difficult to find. Bring both shoulders slightly inward and lean forward to shorten the body-to-racket distance. Flatten the racket face slightly at contact.

review_notes: The repeated fragment suggests something is too far back, but the Chinese does not identify it and the English interprets it as backward leaning. A reliable technical comment cannot be reconstructed.

comment_en: Your wrist force and overall force application are good, but the waist is too upright. Lean forward and open the inward-folded racket position by adjusting the hand slightly backward. Keep the hand aligned with the forearm at 180 degrees rather than folding it to a smaller angle.

Your forearm closing produces a very good explosive burst, but contact is too far back and you sometimes lose the ball's position. Move your feet and contact point forward and meet the ball near its peak with both brushing and impact. Relax the forearm and wrist during preparation, tightening only at contact for a cleaner burst. Turn the right hip back with the waist and let the waist lead the arm into forearm closing instead of relying mainly on arm force.

Your center of gravity is too high and too far back on the heels. Bend the knees forward, feel the toes gripping the ground and shift slightly right before contact and left afterward. The backswing has improved, but take it backward rather than downward and keep the forearm raised. Open the inward-folded racket position outward and backward. Lower the upper body, soften the chest and bring both shoulders slightly inward.

review_notes: The source contains only repeated encouragement to continue practicing, without technical feedback.

comment_en: Your center of gravity is too high and the upper body does not bend enough, leaving the weight unsupported by a stable lower body. Lean forward, feel the forefeet gripping the ground and stabilize the stance. Open the wrist backward at contact preparation rather than taking a downward backswing. Soften the overly upright chest and waist and bring both shoulders slightly inward to connect the movement.

Because you are tall, lower your center of gravity more. Your head repeatedly turns right with the ball; keep it upright and facing forward while tracking the ball to find contact more easily. Relax the right shoulder, contact the ball earlier and use more waist force.

Your center of gravity is too high, especially in the lower body, forcing the forearm into a downward backswing. Bend the knees to lower your body, raise the forearm slightly and turn the waist backward to prepare the stroke.

Widen your stance and lower your center of gravity to account for your height. Reduce the excessive head movement and keep the head upright and facing forward. Your forearm closing force is good; add a stronger, more explosive waist rotation to it.

Bend your knees more to lower your high center of gravity. Raise the forearm slightly and turn the waist backward to prepare the force. Limit head rotation while tracking the ball; the coach advises watching it pass rather than turning the head all the way until racket contact, as that can delay the response to faster balls.

Your weight moves around too much in the latter half. Keep it steadier and lower your high center of gravity. Relax the right shoulder, increase the tight distance between the wrist and waist and keep the head upright and facing forward. Your forearm closing force is very good; combine it with more explosive waist force.

Lower your center of gravity with more knee bend. Raise the forearm for a backward preparation instead of letting it drop naturally, then reduce its excessive movement during the hit. Lift the right shoulder slightly and keep the head facing the opponent without excessive turning.

Your body rises and falls too much. Settle into a stable stance and keep the weight steady. Contact the ball earlier in defense, relax the right shoulder and give the elbow more space from the waist. Shorten the swing.
Lower your high center of gravity and feel the weight on the forefeet. Your shoulder is too loose and lets the forearm drop during preparation. Raise the forearm and right shoulder slightly.

Keep your center of gravity steady instead of rising and falling. The contact timing is good early in the clip but becomes late; maintain the earlier timing. Relax the right shoulder as the strokes continue and open the cramped space between the arm joint and waist.
review_notes: The source recommends two to three fists of spacing but calls it the shoulder-to-waist distance, leaving the intended anatomical reference unclear.

comment_en: Lower your high lower-body position and raise the forearm slightly instead of letting it drop in the backswing. Limit head rotation while tracking the ball; the coach advises watching it pass rather than turning all the way until the ball reaches the racket.

You stand higher than in the previous two clips. Sink lower, relax the stiff right shoulder and increase the tight space between the elbow and waist by reaching the hand slightly farther out. Shorten the overly long stroke.

Bend your knees more to lower your high center of gravity. The forearm becomes too loose during recovery; keep it slightly raised and return along the same path as the stroke instead of making a circle. Limit excessive head turning and avoid following the ball with the head all the way to racket contact.

Your step-in action is excellent, but the waist, right shoulder and right upper arm are stiff. Relax the upper body, close the racket angle and use the wrist to brush more, improving the stroke's stability.

Your center of gravity is high. Lean the upper body forward into the table and bring the upper arm closer to the torso. The large angle between them and excessive upper-arm force make the stroke too big to control well. Let the forearm lead the upper arm and keep the action compact.
Your shoulder and arm remain somewhat stiff; relax them.

Your contact point and explosive force are good. Shorten the overall action, especially by reducing the large angle between the upper arm and torso. Lean farther into the table to close that distance and control the ball more with the forearm.
Your right shoulder remains stiff. Step in earlier and move the late contact timing forward as well. Add more brushing at contact.

Lean forward at the waist, soften the chest and draw in the abdomen. Reduce the oversized backswing and direct more of the movement forward. Avoid excessive upper-arm force and feel the forearm leading the upper arm.

Open the upper arm, forearm and wrist farther from the body; the action still feels cramped despite some forearm backswing. Relax the upper arm and shoulder during preparation and carry the stroke farther through contact to release the force fully. Keep the racket face flatter and more consistent instead of alternating between upright and flat. Settle into a stable stance after serving rather than letting the weight sway.

Your overall serve and force application are good. Open the left palm flat instead of curling the hand around the toss. The low toss makes you miss the best contact point, puts the first bounce too close to your body and causes errors or a high arc. Raising the toss in the latter half solves these problems well.

Your forearm backswing is shorter than in the previous clip, and the action is cramped and stiff. Relax the upper arm and lengthen the preparation. Flatten the overly upright racket face so that contact moves from its front portion toward the center. Stabilize your stance after the serve. You try to use the waist, but the tight arm prevents either source of force from reaching the ball effectively; relax and apply waist and arm force together.

Your overall serve is sound. Open the left palm flat before tossing instead of curling it up. Focus on finding the best contact timing, since contacting too early or too late produces errors or a poor arc.

Your elbow preparation is still too short, even shorter than in the first clip. Relax and increase the space between the upper arm and body to lengthen the backswing. Flatten the racket face and brush rather than hitting from a very short preparation. Your waist contributes less effectively than before; relax the body as you bend and engage the abdomen, allowing the elbow and waist to apply force together. Keep your weight stable after serving.

Place the ball in the center of the left palm and open the hand flat before tossing upward. Holding it on the fingers or curling them can send the toss sideways. Your overall serve is sound, but find the contact timing more accurately. A higher toss may give you more time to do so.
Relax the stiff shoulder and upper arm and contact the ball earlier. Use more wrist force to brush the ball, moving from high to low instead of following the current upward path.

Your action is too large and your weight leans backward. Bend forward at the waist and lean slightly into the table. Reduce the oversized backswing and overall stroke while directing more of the action forward through contact.

Relax the shoulder and contact the ball earlier, rather than too far back. Move the hand forward and the forearm downward instead of lifting upward. Use stronger wrist force to brush the lower half of the ball and improve its quality. Reaching the hand forward is enough; do not press the shoulder downward.

Shorten the backswing and go more directly to the ball. Bend the waist and lean your weight forward. Feel a cutting, forward brush from the forearm instead of flinging the upper arm from behind and to the right, which fails to create enough brushing.

Your footwork is less organized and the step-in is less accurate than in the first clip. Contact is still too late; meet the rising ball earlier and brush its underside with a downward action instead of lifting upward. Relax the shoulder and add more wrist force to improve the return's quality.

Control the habitual backward preparation and go directly to the ball with a smaller action. Lean your weight farther into the table, bending the waist instead of keeping it straight, so that the body can control the ball better.

Your other movements and step-in are very good, but the contact is too late and sends the ball high and long. Complete the short touch while the ball is rising to produce a lower, higher-quality return.

Contact the ball just after the bounce rather than at the peak or on the descent. Your weight is too far back; move it onto the right forefoot, bend the waist and lean into the table. Avoid a backward preparation and move forward to meet the ball directly.
Your downward cut lowers the return's arc. Contact the ball earlier, since the current late timing reduces consistency. As you use more wrist action, the shoulder starts to stiffen; keep it relaxed.

Your brushing has improved and gives you good ball control, but contact is still not immediately after the bounce. Lean your weight forward and bend the waist more to feel the body controlling the ball.
