Several strokes use excellent downward wrist pressure and produce low, short returns, but you do not sustain this quality. Contact remains inconsistent and too late, making you use extra force to keep the ball short. Meet it earlier, use more wrist action in the downward touch and relax the shoulder. Your step-in timing is good.

Your contact point has improved, but it is still not just after the bounce. Avoid bending the wrist too far outward; keep it aligned with the forearm at 180 degrees. Let the forearm brush while the wrist provides stable support. Lean the whole body farther forward and feel it leading the forearm to control the ball.

Your forearm closing has good explosive force, but you mainly lift and brush with the hand and shoulder rather than combining waist rotation with the stroke. Turn the waist and hips farther right and let them lead the arm. This should reduce the excessive forearm travel and bring more waist force into contact instead of relying on the shoulder.

Bend the knees more to lower your high center of gravity. Your preparation is too loose, especially through the forearm, which drops downward. Raise it and prepare backward. Keep the arm bent and compact, maintaining angles between the upper arm and forearm and between the upper arm and body rather than extending everything into a straight line.

Your feet become fixed in the latter half, so you fail to adjust to small changes in ball placement. Watch the ball and move the feet first instead of reaching with the body or waist. Reduce the excessive forearm range, turn the waist farther right to lead the forearm and relax the shoulder. Contact earlier and apply waist and forearm force together for better ball quality.

Your center of gravity is too high. Bend lower, lean forward and feel the forefeet and legs gripping the ground. Raise the forearm during preparation and keep the arm and shoulder closer to the body. Avoid straightening the shoulder and arm away from the torso; a compact, bent position will connect the body's force to contact.

You are trying to add power, but the hand travels too far, finishing beside the ear. Stop the stroke in front of the nose and eyes instead of continuing the swing. Bring more waist force into the hit rather than relying mainly on the hand. Wait slightly for the ball to reach its highest point, and relax the stiff shoulder and upper arm.

Your waist rotation and force are fairly good, but the overall action is too large and the body's force does not fully reach the ball at contact. The shoulder is too far from the body, disconnecting the movement. Reduce the angles between the upper arm and torso and between the upper arm and forearm. Keep the preparation bent and compact instead of extending the shoulder and arm into a straight line.

Your preparation is too short. Relax the shoulder, forearm and wrist, turn the waist farther right and close the forearm briefly at contact. The grip is not seated firmly in the web between the thumb and index finger, allowing the wrist to wobble. Secure that contact while keeping the arm relaxed and the body leaning forward.

Your upper body is stiff and your center of gravity is high. Bend the knees more and lean farther forward at the waist. Stabilize the loose wrist, lower it from its raised position and align it with the forearm at about 180 degrees. Reduce the excessive head turning and face the opponent rather than looking down toward your racket.

Your center of gravity rises as you continue playing. Maintain a forward lean, turn the waist earlier and allow a longer backswing. For this attacking stroke, drive from back to front with more direct impact and less brushing to increase ball speed.

Your waist rotation and transfer have improved. Lower the high hand position and feel the index finger pressing against the racket face to apply force. Lower the upper body and raise the backswing slightly for better force production. Lift the hanging left elbow and arm to roughly a 90-degree position to balance the two sides of the body.
review_notes: The English source reverses the Chinese instruction about index-finger pressure; the merged text follows the Chinese.

comment_en: Both shoulders are very stiff. Relax the left hand and keep it beside the body. Take the hand and waist together to the right, close the forearm and finish with the body leaning forward. Avoid bending the wrist too far backward, refine the contact timing and recover earlier.

Your forehand wrist is too stiff, apparently because of the grip. Seat the racket handle against the web between the thumb and index finger instead of toward the middle, ring and little fingers. This should free the wrist and make index-finger force easier to feel. Your weight position, raised non-playing arm, stroke fluency and rhythm have improved, but lean farther forward at the waist to lower the upper body.

You rise upright as the rally continues. Maintain a forward lean and relax the stiff shoulder, upper arm, forearm and wrist. Let the shoulder provide a stable connection while you prepare and then move forward to borrow the opponent's force, rather than generating all the force yourself.

Your body is too tense, which may be preventing recovery and making the contact rushed. Relax before the hit. Move the right foot back so that the left is slightly ahead, bend the knees and lean forward. Increase the small preparation and wait until the ball reaches its highest point instead of hitting immediately after the bounce.
review_notes: Although filed under block, the coach refers to a forehand attack in the stance instruction.

comment_en: Plant the foot firmly and establish stability when stepping in.

Your recovery is faster and more balls land on the table. However, you still step the right foot forward to apply force; keep it level with the left or slightly behind. Lower your high center of gravity, bend the overly straight waist and relax the body so that waist and shoulder force can combine. Lower the excessively high wrist movement.
Your center of gravity rises as you play. Keep the weight leaning forward. After preparing backward, press forward using the opponent's force rather than generating the force yourself.

Stepping the right foot forward limits the upper body's backward rotation and prevents lower-body force from transferring upward. Relax before contact instead of remaining stiff throughout, which prevents an explosive release.
Contact the ball a little earlier and recover sooner before stepping in again. Reduce the oversized forearm action and use more wrist brushing.

Your body is too stiff, leaving both preparation and recovery incomplete. Lower the raised wrist and align it with the forearm at about 180 degrees. Bend the knees, lean forward at the waist and keep the weight on the forefeet. Center the grip in the web between the thumb and index finger rather than biasing it toward either finger; your thumb-side bias appears to make the wrist tilt upward.

Bring the left shoulder slightly inward and let it follow the ball with the movement. Contact earlier, shorten the oversized action and use more wrist force with less forearm movement. Relax the stiff right shoulder.

Your familiarity has improved, but the technique has not. You still fling the wrist, preventing effective index-finger force; lower the racket head. The racket is too far from the upper body and the shoulder seems to act alone. Let the upper body lead the whole stroke and relax before applying force instead of remaining stiff throughout.

Your weight and both shoulders tend to lean backward. Keep the body leaning forward while allowing the racket to tilt back for brushing. Add more preparation, relax the stiff wrist and shoulder and use a brief wrist burst to brush the ball.

You miss the intended contact point. Arrange the timing and position so that contact is around the one-o'clock direction. Lower your high center of gravity, lean the upper body farther forward and bend the stiff, upright waist. Lower the excessively raised wrist.
review_notes: The description of the current hitting direction contains inconsistent clock positions; only the clear one-o'clock target is retained.

comment_en: Your hand swing is too small; increase the backswing without suddenly lifting the upper arm and elbow. Keep the shoulder and upper arm supported and use a compact, brief action to add sidespin rather than tensing the whole arm at once. Settle into a stable stance after serving.

Place the ball in the center of the left palm and finish the serve with weight on the left leg. Open the forearm farther outward during the toss to allow more force at contact. If the intended serve is side-topspin, keep the racket face more upright; an overly flat face produces side-underspin instead.

Plant the feet firmly during the serve, then lean the weight forward afterward. Keep the shoulder and wrist prepared rather than suddenly lifting them. Increase the forearm backswing and flatten the racket face. Move the contact point slightly forward from its overly inward position and apply a brief brushing force instead of relying mainly on impact.

Your brushing is good and your weight position has improved. Land the left foot at the instant of contact to help the waist and hips rotate and contribute force. Lower the upper-body position before the serve, lean farther forward at the waist and open the right forearm farther outward after the toss. These changes should improve power, speed and spin.

Prepare earlier by taking the forearm back and tilting the hand slightly backward. Relax the shoulder and have the arm and elbow set in advance, then tighten the forearm and wrist to apply force. Keep the feet still until after contact. During recovery, reset the racket face together with the rest of the action.
review_notes: The source also requests an instantaneous backward or inward waist action during the serve, but its timing and intended direction are unclear.

comment_en: Your serving familiarity is good and the footwork has improved considerably, but the upper-body position remains too high. As you apply force forward, commit the weight more fully onto the left leg and make the left-foot landing clearer.

Contact the ball and step the right foot forward earlier. Your wrist action is very good, but stop it after the stroke rather than immediately pulling it back. Make a clear relaxed-to-firm grip transition instead of remaining loose. Lean the whole body forward, bringing the left shoulder with it so that you can control the ball rather than leaving that shoulder behind.
Lean the upper body farther forward.

Contact the ball earlier and make the acceleration more pronounced. Firm the grip through the stroke instead of flinging the racket loosely. Prepare backward with the forearm before moving forward, and keep the weight leaning forward.
review_notes: The source's description of the left shoulder alternates between inward and outward positioning and cannot be resolved.

comment_en: Your wrist action is generally sound, but make it more stable at contact. Hold the racket firmly with the fingers and avoid taking the wrist too far back. Raise the left hand slightly for balance and lean farther forward at the overly upright waist.

Your step-in timing improves and becomes increasingly accurate later in the clip. The timing of the wrist burst is good, but increase its acceleration for a more explosive action. Open the right elbow slightly away from the body instead of keeping it tucked in, and lean the whole body forward.

The racket shakes after contact, suggesting that the grip is loose and forces you to keep adjusting the face. Secure the grip, especially around the thumb and index finger, before hitting. Your force application and contact point are sound. Raise the left hand for better balance and lean the upper body farther forward.

The action is stiff and too small; take the wrist and forearm slightly farther back. Use both feet to adjust toward the ball and bring the left shoulder forward with the upper body instead of leaving it behind. Flatten the racket face slightly and contact the ball earlier, before it has dropped too far.

Your contact point and brushing are good. The main issue is positioning: start from the backhand side or middle, rather than the forehand side, and step the right foot forward into the table instead of outside its edge. Lean the upper body farther forward and shorten the distance between the body and racket.

Your wrist preparation is too short and the forearm does too much of the work. Add a clearer, brief wrist burst after preparing the forearm. Later you adjust with both feet, which is better than reaching with only one step; use both feet to find the ball. Keep the weight forward, bring the left shoulder with the body and open the tucked-in elbow to free the action.

Your brushing is fairly good, but the main problems are the starting position and step-in. Stand nearer the middle or backhand side and step the right foot forward into the table instead of sideways along its edge. Lean the upper body forward and contact the ball just after the bounce; waiting until its peak is too late for the short touch.

Your rhythm is disorganized. Start moving both feet earlier, open the wrist during preparation and coordinate the arm and wrist for a stronger explosive action. Keep the weight forward and avoid leaving the left shoulder far behind. Hold the racket face more upright as you brush the underside of the ball.

Your contact point, brushing and forehand shoulder action are sound. The main issue is the stance and step-in. Start on the left side of the table or in the middle and reach the shoulder diagonally forward and right, rather than starting on the forehand side and stepping straight forward to push the ball.

Relax the hand, arm, shoulder and wrist and make softer contact instead of repeatedly bumping the ball. Load the right foot and lower yourself by bending the legs rather than sitting backward. Keep the weight pressing forward through the waist turn and finish, and contact the ball earlier.
review_notes: Fragments about the side of the hips and downward pressure do not identify a precise adjustment reliably.

comment_en: Your lower-body weight control and waist and hip rotation are fairly good. The main problems are in the upper body: lean farther forward at the waist and adjust the grip. The current grip makes the wrist stiff and leaves the middle, ring and little fingers supplying the force. Seat the handle securely toward the thumb-index web without a gap so that you can feel the index finger applying force.

Turn a little farther right during the backswing, load the right foot and bend the right knee more to lower the body. Your brief explosive waist turn is good. Press the racket forward with a slightly flatter face and feel the brushing along the side of the ball. Keep the racket action consistent through the finish instead of turning it, and maintain forward weight rather than leaning backward.

The main problems remain in the upper body. Lower the wrist and secure the grip before contact, not after touching the ball. Bend forward, soften the chest and draw in the abdomen. Apply waist and shoulder force together without a delay so that both reach the ball at the same instant.

review_notes: The source contains only the placeholder 'comment1', with no technical feedback.

comment_en: You consciously lean forward before the stroke but return to the previous upright habit during play. The straight waist leaves the shoulder too far from the body and the forearm preparation too low. Lean forward so that the racket rises naturally and the whole action connects. Your force level and timing are otherwise fairly good.

Your shoulder does unnecessary work while the waist contributes too little. Relax the shoulder, stabilize the core and let the waist lead the rotation. Prepare over a longer distance, apply forearm force earlier and close it more completely. Keep the core steady while the waist rotates from side to side, with a clear sequence to the action.

Stabilize the weight near the middle as the hips rotate instead of letting the buttocks drive the waist and hips. Bend the knees more to lower the high lower-body position. Contact the ball slightly in front and to the right rather than directly at the side. Lower the raised upper arm and shoulder, letting the right shoulder settle slightly.

Keep the core more upright while leaning forward, and let the waist lead the hand instead of relying only on the shoulder. Begin the backswing earlier. Move the right foot behind the left rather than keeping it in front.

Your weight moves too far from side to side. Keep it centered and rotate from the right rear toward the left front rather than swaying laterally. Lower the forearm slightly during preparation instead of lifting it backward. Contact around the two-o'clock position rather than the late three-o'clock position. Your rhythm is too rigid; adjust the waist and hips to the incoming ball.

Lower your high center of gravity through the legs instead of excessively pitching the torso forward. You still use too much shoulder force; relax the shoulder during preparation and turn the waist backward without dropping it. Lengthen the forearm backswing and closing action, relax the upper arm and allow roughly two to three fists of space from the body. Strike from back to front with direct impact rather than trying to brush.

Your rhythm has improved, but insufficient knee bend leaves the upper and lower body disconnected. Bend the knees and keep the weight on the forefeet. Keep the torso centered instead of leaning the whole upper body right; only the right shoulder needs to settle slightly. Stabilize the core and rotate the hips forward from the center rather than driving them by swaying the buttocks sideways.

Keep the feet parallel rather than placing the right foot ahead of the left. Maintain a slight forward lean without shifting the weight forward during the waist turn. Move the wrist and arm farther from the body and relax the wrist. Use a little waist rotation to borrow the incoming force, then direct forearm force forward instead of using the wrist. Avoid dropping the shoulder.

The angles between the upper arm and forearm and between the upper arm and torso are too small. Open the forearm and maintain a suitable angle through contact. Keep the upper body and hips centered, allowing only a slight lowering of the right shoulder. Avoid swaying the hips sideways as you turn the waist.
review_notes: The source describes excessive rightward weight causing excessive leftward movement; the precise sequence is unclear.

comment_en: You lower the shoulder during preparation instead of turning sufficiently backward through the waist. Tighten and stabilize the core so that the hips do not swing around. Move the wrist farther from the body, open the arm and use the incoming ball's force. Relax the shoulder and forearm.

You begin with centered weight but habitually shift too far left during contact. Keep the hips centered and rotate from the right rear toward the left front rather than swaying sideways. Open the cramped forehand arm position, enlarge the action and finish toward the left eyebrow. At this learning stage, establish a complete, standard movement before prioritizing the percentage of balls landing on the table.

Your shoulder drops too much and the wrist moves increasingly close to the body. Open the action to leave roughly two to three fists of space. Draw back to absorb the incoming force rather than tapping with the wrist, and use a longer stroke. Rotate backward and right instead of tipping the body to the right.

The previous issues remain. Stabilize the core, bend the right knee slightly and adjust the weight rightward to counter the excessive leftward lean. Open the angles between the forearm and upper arm and between the upper arm and torso. Increase the latter angle through contact to complete the action smoothly.
review_notes: A source fragment also names the left knee without completing its instruction; the right-knee correction is repeated clearly.

comment_en: Your upper body is stiff and the stroke lacks brushing. Move the wrist farther from the body, prepare it slightly backward and open the forearm to lift the ball. Keep the shoulder from dropping and hold the core centered instead of leaning right.

You have not found the flick's force application, so shortening the movement leaves you unable to produce an effective stroke. You rely almost entirely on the upper arm, with little forearm or wrist force. Bring the arm more forward to reduce the large angle from the torso and improve force transfer to the ball.

Your upper body remains stiff and the elbow is tucked inward. Open it outward and relax. Reach the hand farther forward instead of keeping it too close to the body, press the weight forward and add more wrist brushing. Avoid dropping the shoulder.

You flick mainly with the upper arm and shoulder-elbow action. Open the elbow outward instead of folding it inward over the table. Relax the shoulder, elbow and upper arm and use the fingers, wrist and forearm. Keep the weight centered rather than leaning left, with only a slight forward-right inclination.
Turn the elbow slightly outward and relax the arm. Lean forward and use more wrist force to brush upward rather than lifting the whole arm.

You have adjusted the movement, but the force has shifted from the upper arm to the shoulder and elbow rather than to the fingers and wrist. Control the ball's height with the wrist and fingers instead of lifting it with the whole arm. Open the inward-folded elbow to free that action. Your weight is too far into the table; move both feet back about half a step to create room for a stroke from behind toward the front and upward.

Your shoulder, upper arm, forearm, elbow and wrist are stiff. Relax the wrist first so that it can produce a brief burst. Move the elbow away from the body and open the forearm to create room for preparation. Apply a sudden impact with a slightly more upright face, keeping the wrist from flinging and the racket angle from flipping upward or backward. Stand firmly during contact and press the body forward afterward.

Your overall action is good, but the weight transfer needs improvement. The coach asks for the toss to start below the table rather than above it. Keep the racket face more vertical, open the forearm and upper arm sufficiently and lengthen the contact to increase spin.
review_notes: The below-table toss instruction is retained as stated; it conflicts with above-table toss advice in this coach's later files.

comment_en: Your body is stiff and the wrist folds too far inward. Open the wrist and elbow, increase the short forearm preparation and use a brief wrist burst at contact. Extend the forearm forward afterward instead of keeping it tucked in. Relax the shoulder and move contact inward from the racket tip toward the upper-middle part of the face for better control. Press forward rather than finishing upward.

Your weight transfer is good, but contact is too brief. For side-topspin, contact the side of the ball with a vertical racket face rather than its rear. Toss from above the table, without taking the left hand below it. Finish with the weight farther left instead of centered so that the body, hand and shoulder can contribute together.

Stabilize the weight after serving and lower it through both legs. Relax the tight wrist and both shoulders. Enlarge the action, take the forearm farther back and extend it forward through contact with a little more impact force. Wait for the ball to drop slightly farther before hitting.

Your weight transfer has improved, but the short contact produces weak spin. Toss from above the table instead of starting with the left hand below it. Maintain a more vertical racket face and contact the side of the ball rather than its rear. Increase the backward shoulder preparation; the coach specifically asks for more upward and backward movement through the left shoulder to improve spin and speed.
review_notes: The source names the left shoulder in the preparation instruction; this potentially unusual anatomical reference is preserved for review.

comment_en: Your wrist bends too far backward. Bring it forward to align more closely with the forearm and make its brief force more distinct. Relax both shoulders and make the forward and backward weight movement clearer.

Your overall action and weight control are good, and the contact timing is not late. Aim to meet the ball at its highest point. Keep the wrist and forearm stable in a straight, 180-degree alignment instead of bending the wrist either way or leaving it loose. Only small adjustments are needed.

Keep the core steadier and avoid a wobbling, circular movement. Lean the weight forward without excessive waist effort. Take the right forearm back for preparation and make the wrist's explosive force more distinct. Relax both shoulders.
review_notes: The English source is heavily corrupted. Instructions about spacing, the step-in and body-force initiation cannot be reconstructed reliably, and the two language fields differ.

comment_en: Your force application is good and the weight is stable. Lower and stabilize the wrist so that contact is on the upper-right part of the racket face rather than its lower part. Meet the ball slightly earlier at its highest point instead of just after, where combining force and brushing are less effective.

Contact the ball earlier instead of waiting until it has risen high and begun descending. Open the inward-folded wrist and combine brief forearm and wrist force. The forearm force is sufficient; add more from the wrist. Relax both shoulders and the grip, widen the narrow foot spacing and keep the left hand beside the body. Add a clear step forward and recovery backward.

Let the forearm lead the upper arm. Bring the racket face to the ball first rather than extending the upper arm ahead of it, allowing the racket to lead the shoulder into contact. Your low weight position is well controlled, but move the upper body slightly back to leave enough space for contact and make the timing easier to manage.

Your elbow is more open than before, but you are no longer using enough forearm. Bring the forearm into the action to provide stability and coordinate it with a brief wrist burst. Contact earlier, accelerate the wrist more clearly and relax the shoulder.

Your upper body is too low and forward. Bend the right knee more and adjust the upper-body weight slightly backward. Contact is too late; meet the ball just after the bounce. Start nearer the middle or backhand side instead of the forehand side.

Relax the shoulder instead of reaching it forward. Put the weight on the right foot, recover and return to that foot for the next ball rather than stepping onto the left. Add a little more forearm backswing, then use a brief wrist burst. Finish with the racket head facing forward instead of moving sideways.

Your upper body leans too far into the table. Move it slightly back, bend the right knee more and relax the stiff posture, while allowing the right shoulder to reach a little forward. Contact the short ball just after the bounce rather than at its peak. Start nearer the middle or backhand side and step the right foot diagonally forward into the table instead of sideways outside its edge.

Your forearm preparation is too short. Step the feet farther forward to move the weight into position instead of only leaning the torso excessively over the table. Lengthen the forearm backswing and use more wrist action. Finish with the racket head pointing forward rather than sideways, and relax the shoulder.

Your contact point has improved but remains late; meet the ball just after the bounce. Start nearer the middle or slightly toward the backhand side instead of the forehand side. Move the upper body slightly back from its excessive reach into the table, bend the knees and support the weight through the legs. Let the knees extend toward the table instead of reaching with the upper body and head.

Your rhythm is disorganized and you repeatedly sink the shoulder to hit. Load the right foot, bend the right leg and turn the waist right instead of powering the stroke through the shoulder. Relax the shoulder and hand, and release the forearm's premature tension before combining the waist turn with the stroke.

Your weight sways too much and the stance is not settled. Feel the toes gripping the ground and prevent excessive side-to-side movement or body tilting. Keep the left arm near the torso with a controlled angle instead of moving the left shoulder excessively before contact. Stabilize the hips and legs within a moderate range; the upper-body waist and shoulder rotation are otherwise fairly good.

Keep the left hand beside the body instead of reaching it forward. Move the right foot slightly back to create room for waist rotation, and let the shoulder lower with that turn. Relax the forearm, shoulder and wrist during preparation, make a clear relaxed-to-firm burst and then relax again. Move the contact point forward from its late position.
review_notes: The source describes tightening after contact, leaving the exact timing of the force burst unclear.

comment_en: Your weight is more stable for the first few balls but becomes unstable again later. Lower the body, bend the knees farther forward and down and feel the toes gripping the ground. Keep the feet steady with less floating movement. The right shoulder's action and force are good, but prevent the left shoulder from swinging right with the waist. Keep the left upper arm beside the body at a controlled angle.

You still rely too much on the shoulder and right upper arm. Relax before applying force, keep the left hand from reaching forward and sink through the right leg during the turn. Stabilize the core without swaying sideways, lean slightly forward and combine abdominal engagement with a brief wrist burst and firm grip.
review_notes: The final fragments about leg, arm and joint force are unclear; the English also differs on whether upper-arm force is an observation or a recommendation.

comment_en: Lower your lower-body center of gravity to keep the feet from shifting back and forth during play.
review_notes: The Chinese source is cut off mid-sentence; the complete English field supplies the consequence about foot movement.

comment_en: Your impact is sound, but the wrist makes a backward circle during preparation. Keep it in a consistent position instead of moving it around. For the forehand attack, use more waist rotation and forearm impact rather than excessive wrist force, and relax the shoulder.

Your upper-body position and contact feel are good, but lower the high lower-body center of gravity. Increase the short backswing and bring more waist and hip rotation into contact so that the body's force reaches the ball.
review_notes: The Chinese fields are corrupted. This paragraph uses the readable English fields; the final description of a flat center of gravity is unclear.

comment_en: Your weight becomes less stable later in the clip. Keep it centered and prepare with waist rotation rather than swaying. Stop the wrist from making a circle before contact. Use the waist turn and forearm closing to produce the forehand attack, keeping the wrist stable.

Bend the knees more to lower the high lower-body center of gravity. Increase the limited waist rotation and backward preparation. Feel the upper arm actively drawing back and give the loading phase more range so that more force reaches the ball.

Increase the small backward waist turn. Finish the stroke in front of the nose and stop promptly instead of continuing too far, then prepare for the next ball. The right-foot position looks awkward; moving it slightly back may help. Relax during preparation, make the forearm closing more instantaneous and keep the wrist still. Stabilize the weight instead of swaying from side to side.

Your lower-body center of gravity is high. Bend the right leg more and turn the right knee outward before contact to help the upper body prepare backward instead of standing straight and fixed. Feel the left leg driving against the ground to apply force forward.

Prepare earlier and enlarge the backswing. Your right foot creeps forward as you play; keep it slightly behind to allow waist rotation and preparation. Make the forearm closing a brief burst, avoid adding wrist force and relax the shoulder.

Your lower-body center of gravity is high and the weight falls backward after contact. Bend both knees and keep the weight on the forefeet. Let the body lead the shoulder instead of hitting with the hand while the body stays still, and feel the whole body leaning forward to press through the ball.

Your backswing is too short and the stroke looks like tossing the ball. Increase the preparation with waist rotation and control the finish. Recover through the forearm rather than the wrist. Stabilize the core, keep the weight forward and relax the shoulders.
review_notes: A separate fragment says not to draw backward, contradicting the instruction to lengthen the backswing; its intended scope is unclear.

comment_en: Shift slightly right before contact and bend the right knee more. After the hit, move forward and left instead of leaning left from the outset. Relax and feel the body leading the shoulder so that the two remain connected.

Use less independent hand force and press forward to borrow the incoming ball's force. The wrist moves too much; hold it steady like a fixed pivot while the forearm presses forward. Keep the core engaged and stable.

Your center of gravity remains high because the knees do not bend enough. Bend the right knee fully before contact, then feel the knees turning toward the left front afterward. Make the action more compact and include waist rotation so that the body's force reaches contact, rather than only swinging the arm.

You find the contact point well, but stand too far forward and stay crowded against the ball. Add a recovery backward before moving forward again. Relax the stiff wrist and flick upward with a brush along the side of the ball instead of driving directly from back to front. Relax the shoulder rather than holding it raised.

Stand near the middle, slightly toward the forehand side, and keep the ball in front of the body. Your upper arm and forearm are too stiff. Feel the wrist leading the forearm instead of letting the upper arm drive the entire movement.

Incline the racket face forward to brush the ball. Relax the shoulder and keep the wrist from wobbling. Reach the position by stepping and pressing the body slightly forward instead of stretching the wrist toward the ball. Add a recovery backward and another forward step. Use an upward wrist brush rather than a direct backward-to-forward hit.

Your action is stiff. Bring the elbow slightly inward and closer to the body rather than turning it too far outward. Relax the right shoulder, step the right foot forward and lean the weight diagonally forward and right. Let the wrist lead the forearm and upper arm instead of powering the stroke through the upper arm.

You mainly take the wrist back and hit directly forward. Prepare it slightly downward and use an upward burst to brush the ball instead. Move the feet to find space, as standing still leaves the early balls crowded against the body. Relax the shoulder, open the elbow slightly, prepare the forearm backward and use more wrist action. Make the inconsistent contact point a little earlier.

Contact the ball slightly in front and to the right rather than directly at your side. Reduce the angle between the upper arm and torso and turn the elbow slightly inward before contact. Avoid flaring it outward, which encourages excessive upper-arm force, so that you can feel the forearm and wrist working.

Lower the excessively raised elbow and take the forearm farther back before applying a brief burst. For this spin-heavy serve, keep the first bounce closer to you on your own side. Use a flatter racket angle to brush the side of the ball for stronger spin.

comment_en: Lower your high center of gravity and stand with the left foot forward and the right behind, bending the right knee more. Toss from the center of the left palm rather than the fingers. Keep the upper arm close to the body and apply forward force with the forearm and wrist instead of the upper arm. Adjust the serving grip by moving the middle, ring and little fingers to the right side of the racket rather than wrapping them fully around it, freeing the stiff wrist to open outward before contact.

Your elbow is still held too high, causing excessive shoulder effort. Lower and relax it, use more of the body's force and find a comfortable release. Open the left hand flat for the toss instead of holding the ball in curled fingers. Flatten the racket face slightly at contact.

You serve mainly with the shoulder rather than using the body's force. Stand with the left foot ahead and begin with weight on the left leg. Shift slightly backward and right after the toss, then return left at contact; a left-foot landing can help. Lower the raised right shoulder and elbow, keep the upper arm close to the body and use forearm and wrist force instead of flaring the elbow upward.

Add more brushing to the serve. Later you increasingly hit the ball directly, making it rise higher. Open the left palm flat for the toss, lower the raised shoulder and elbow and combine more forearm force with the wrist. Relax the shoulder and flatten the racket face to brush the ball.

Your brief force at contact is good, but the serving movement needs correction. Reduce the angle between the upper arm and torso and keep the elbow inward. The backswing is too short because the waist does not rotate enough. During the toss, use the waist to carry the arm and racket backward and up above the right shoulder. As you apply force forward, avoid lifting the shoulder and elbow; let them settle downward. Add a left-foot landing to complete the weight transfer.

Your overall stroke is good. Add clearer footwork, recovering backward after contact and moving forward again for the next ball. Increase the wrist's brief force and open it slightly outward to allow better forearm preparation.

Your overall technique is sound. The main adjustment is to control the push with the forearm rather than the wrist. Stabilize the wrist and feel the forearm controlling the ball for greater consistency.

Your overall stroke is very good. Shorten the action so that its force is less dispersed, and make the wrist's relaxed-to-firm transition more explosive. You can find the ball without much adjustment in this clip, but still establish a clear forward step and backward recovery.
Keep the wrist and forearm in a stable, straight 180-degree alignment throughout contact. Prepare backward with the forearm instead of the wrist, and flatten the racket face slightly.
Your overall movement is very good and the action size is appropriate. Add more wrist force and move the late contact point forward.

Your overall action and brushing are very good, but several errors come from excessive wrist use. Hold the racket firmly with the fingers to stabilize the wrist and feel the forearm applying force instead of relying too much on the wrist.

Your wrist contributes too little and you only touch the ball lightly, making it difficult to lower the arc. Firm the grip and use some wrist action to cut downward. Move the feet more to find the ball's position.

comment_en: Your stance and weight control are good. Meet the ball just after the bounce on your side instead of at its highest point, because poor timing makes the short return difficult to control. Tilt the racket face slightly back rather than keeping it vertical. Stabilize the wrist relative to the forearm and let the forearm control the stroke. Carry it slightly forward to lengthen contact and brush the ball instead of merely touching it.

Your footwork is disorganized for the first few balls and you do not find the position, but the movement becomes good once you settle into place. Increase the preparation slightly and firm the grip at contact, using a clearer wrist burst to press the ball's arc lower. The other aspects are good.

Contact the ball just after the bounce, since even a slight delay makes it harder to control. Viewed from the side, keep the wrist and forearm in a straight line without lifting the wrist excessively. Control the ball with the forearm rather than the wrist.
Your backswing is still too small. Prepare more fully and make the burst of arm force clearer. The arm looks cramped against the body; move it slightly outward to free the action.

Contact is too brief, leaving too little brushing and sending the ball high. Keep the wrist aligned with the forearm and lower the index finger slightly to feel its force. Let the forearm lead the wrist through contact rather than actively powering the stroke with the wrist, and relax before applying force.

Lift the ball through brushing rather than dragging it upward. Increase the short preparation by turning the waist farther, lowering the body and loading the right foot. Stop the racket after contact instead of extending the swing unnecessarily, then recover promptly.

Lower your center of gravity and enlarge the insufficient backward and rightward preparation through waist rotation. Your action is stiff and the right shoulder is held too high. Let it settle and relax before applying force instead of holding the whole shoulder tense, which restricts power.

Your waist rotation and backward preparation are too small. Turn the waist more and lower the hand during preparation. Shorten the overly long movement after contact and avoid continuing upward. Keep your weight leaning forward through the finish.
Your movement is stiff and the right shoulder is high. Lower the shoulder and action, bend the knees to lower your center of gravity and relax before applying force.

Fewer strokes have a good rhythm than before. Increase the limited waist turn and lengthen the forearm backswing. Relax the shoulder, hand and forearm, then stop the racket after contact. Keep the weight leaning forward instead of collapsing backward after the topspin stroke.

Your waist and hip rotation have improved considerably, but the body falls backward, especially after contact. Finish with the weight toward the left front rather than the left rear, feeling the forefoot on the ground instead of shifting onto the left heel. Relax and lower the stiff right shoulder so that it sits below the left. Stay relaxed before contact, apply force through the hit and relax again afterward.
